lessons.title: Design the two-tier trust hierarchy
lessons.summary: The root establishes trust. The subordinate, also called the issuing CA in this design, handles approved end-entity certificates. Keeping these roles separate protects the root from daily network exposure.
steps: Draw the hierarchy: offline standalone root → enterprise issuing CA → approved server/client certificates. There is no network connection to the root.

Record final host and CA names, key provider, algorithm, key sizes, hashes, validity periods, renewal owners, and recovery arrangements. Start from this lab's example values in the next step and change any that your own policy requires: they are examples, not universal requirements.

Example values for this lab: the root CA uses an RSA 4096 key with SHA-256 and a 20-year certificate, and publishes a base CRL every 26 weeks with an overlap period and no delta CRL, refreshed at each offline ceremony. The issuing CA uses RSA 4096 (3072 at minimum) with SHA-256 and a 10-year certificate, a weekly base CRL, and a daily delta CRL. End-entity certificates last one to two years. NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 rates RSA 2048 at 112 bits of security, which it accepts for new signatures only through 2030, so a CA that will still be signing after 2030 uses at least 3072 bits (128 bits of security); Windows Server 2025 requires at least 2,048-bit RSA for TLS server authentication.

Know where each value is set. You choose the key, the hash, and the root's 20-year validity in the AD CS Configuration wizard. Each CA's CAPolicy.inf sets its CRL periods (CRLPeriod, CRLPeriodUnits, CRLDeltaPeriod, CRLDeltaPeriodUnits), which certutil -setreg can change later. The issuing CA's 10-year lifetime is set on the root (CA\ValidityPeriod and CA\ValidityPeriodUnits) before the signing ceremony, because a subordinate CA's lifetime comes from the CA that signs it.

Plan a stable internal publication name such as pki.sbd.test. The Authority Information Access (AIA) location supplies issuer certificates; the CRL Distribution Point (CDP) supplies certificate revocation lists.

Choose the publication host, paths, access rules, and refresh schedule before issuing certificates. Clients inside this air-gapped network must reach those locations without relying on the public internet.
lessons.command:
# Run on the future issuing CA, not the offline root.
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object Name, Domain, PartOfDomain
Resolve-DnsName SBD-DC01.sbd.test
Resolve-DnsName SBD-DC02.sbd.test
lessons.check: The written plan separates trust, issuance, publication, and administration. It identifies who renews CRLs before they expire, and every key size, hash, lifetime, and CRL period has a recorded value and the setting that applies it.
lessons.evidence: Keep the approved hierarchy, the cryptography and lifetime table with the setting that applies each value, and a worksheet mapping every certificate/CRL URL to its actual publisher and file.

model.label: Offline trust
model.text: The root stays outside the live network; signing material is carried to it by hand and the results are carried back.

objectives: Explain why the root stays offline while the issuing CA handles enrollment.
Record the CA identities, cryptography, lifetimes, and CRL periods before installation, starting from this lab's example values.
Plan AIA and CDP publication locations that clients can reach inside the air gap.

quizzes.question: Which role issues routine server certificates in this design?
answers: The offline root for every request
The enterprise issuing CA
The DNS server
quizzes.explanation: The issuing CA handles end-entity enrollment while the offline root signs the approved subordinate CA certificate.

quizzes.question: What do the AIA and CDP locations supply?
answers: Private keys for backup
DNS zone transfers
Issuer certificates and certificate revocation lists
quizzes.explanation: Authority Information Access serves issuer certificates; CRL Distribution Points serve revocation lists. Clients must be able to reach both.

quizzes.question: Why is pki.sbd.test planned before any CA is installed?
answers: Issued certificates embed these URLs, so the publication name must be stable first
The root cannot be installed without it
DNS requires a CNAME before zones replicate
quizzes.explanation: Certificates keep the extensions they were issued with. A stable publication name avoids reissuing everything later.

quizzes.question: In this lab, where is the issuing CA's 10-year certificate lifetime set?
answers: In the issuing CA's own CAPolicy.inf
On the offline root, with CA\ValidityPeriod and CA\ValidityPeriodUnits, before the signing ceremony
In the certificate template for web servers
quizzes.explanation: A subordinate CA's lifetime is set by the CA that signs it. The root's issued-certificate validity settings decide how long the issuing CA's certificate lasts, so they are set and verified before the ceremony.

recap: Trust, issuance, publication, and administration are separated in writing.
Cryptography, names, lifetimes, and CRL periods are approved before installation, starting from this lab's example values.
CRL renewal has a named owner and a date.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 performs the controlled offline root installation.

lessons.title: Configure the offline Root CA
lessons.summary: Treat root installation as a controlled event. Its private key is the highest-value secret in the hierarchy, and its configuration shapes the subordinate certificate it will sign.
steps: Verify SBD-ROOTCA01 is in a workgroup with no active network path. Prepare approved installation media, protected administration, correct time, and backup storage.

Place the reviewed CAPolicy.inf in %SystemRoot% before configuration. Tailor it to the root role: in this lab it sets CRLPeriod=Weeks and CRLPeriodUnits=26, and CRLDeltaPeriodUnits=0 so the root publishes no delta CRL. A self-signed root's own CDP/AIA choices differ from the extensions the root places into issued subordinate certificates.

Install the Certification Authority role with management tools. In the AD CS Configuration wizard choose Standalone CA, Root CA, and a new private key, then apply the approved provider, cryptography (RSA 4096 with SHA-256 in this lab), CA name, validity (20 years), database, and log settings.

Before signing anything, configure the root's issued-certificate AIA/CDP settings, the subordinate validity policy (CA\ValidityPeriod Years and CA\ValidityPeriodUnits 10 in this lab), and the base-CRL schedule (26 weeks with an overlap period, and no delta CRL). Hold requests for explicit approval. Produce and inspect a current root CRL, then capture a protected CA backup.
lessons.command:
# Inspect locally on SBD-ROOTCA01 during the approved root session.
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object Name, Domain, PartOfDomain
Get-Service CertSvc
certutil -getreg CA\CRLPublicationURLs
certutil -getreg CA\CACertPublicationURLs
certutil -getreg CA\ValidityPeriodUnits
certutil -getreg CA\CRLPeriodUnits
lessons.check: The host remains disconnected, the CA is standalone/root, requests require approval, and the planned subordinate URLs and 10-year subordinate validity are configured before signing.
lessons.evidence: Record the root certificate identity, policy file, publication settings, CRL dates, backup location, and operator sign-off. Protect backups containing private keys.
objectives: Verify the disconnected workgroup host before installing the role.
Install a standalone root CA with the approved CAPolicy.inf and settings.
Configure publication URLs and the CRL schedule before signing anything.

quizzes.question: When must the root's issued-certificate publication URLs be configured?
answers: After clients have enrolled
Only after the first CRL expires
Before signing the subordinate CA certificate
quizzes.explanation: Issued certificates retain their extensions. Changing the CA configuration later does not rewrite existing certificates.

quizzes.question: Why is the root a standalone CA rather than an enterprise CA?
answers: Standalone CAs use stronger cryptography
It is not domain-joined and must work disconnected from the directory
Enterprise CAs cannot sign subordinate certificates
quizzes.explanation: An enterprise CA depends on Active Directory. The offline root lives in a workgroup with no network path, so it must be standalone.

quizzes.question: Where does CAPolicy.inf belong before configuration?
answers: The domain SYSVOL share
The removable media only
%SystemRoot% on the CA host
quizzes.explanation: Setup reads CAPolicy.inf from %SystemRoot% during configuration. Placing it afterward does not change the installed CA.

recap: The root host stays disconnected, with controlled media, administration, and time.
CAPolicy.inf is in place before the role is configured.
Publication URLs, validity policy, the CRL schedule, and a protected backup exist before any signing.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 prepares the online issuing CA and its certificate request.

lessons.title: Create the issuing CA request
lessons.summary: Prepare the online issuing server, but keep issuance paused until its CA certificate has been signed and installed. The request carries the public key; the private key stays protected on the issuing system or its approved key provider.
steps: Confirm SBD-SUBCA01 has its final hostname, domain membership, static address, internal DNS, and correct time. Use a dedicated host and the privileges approved for enterprise CA configuration.

Prepare its role-specific CAPolicy.inf (in this lab: CRLPeriod=Weeks, CRLPeriodUnits=1, CRLDeltaPeriod=Days, CRLDeltaPeriodUnits=1, and LoadDefaultTemplates=0) and protected request directory. Decide which templates may later be published instead of enabling a broad default enrollment set.

Install the CA role and management tools. In the AD CS Configuration wizard choose Enterprise CA, Subordinate CA, and the approved new-key/provider settings (RSA 4096 with SHA-256 in this lab). Enter the planned CA identity and storage locations.
Choose Save a certificate request to file. Inspect the resulting request's subject, public key, and CA constraints; record its SHA-256 hash before handing it to the media custodian.
lessons.command:
# Use the actual request path chosen in the wizard.
certutil -dump C:\CAConfig\IssuingCA.req
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\CAConfig\IssuingCA.req
lessons.check: The request matches the approved issuing identity and key profile. The CA is waiting for its signed certificate; do not troubleshoot that expected state by installing another CA.
lessons.evidence: Retain the request, its reviewed fields and hash, and the request-transfer record. Do not place private keys in the transfer package.
objectives: Prepare the domain-joined issuing host with its final identity.
Generate the subordinate CA request without exposing the private key.
Verify and hash the request before it travels to the root.

quizzes.question: What moves to the offline root for signing?
answers: The issuing CA's certificate request
The issuing CA's private key
A network cable connected to the domain
quizzes.explanation: The signed request contains the public key. Root signing does not require exporting the issuing CA private key.

quizzes.question: Why record the request’s SHA-256 hash before the media transfer?
answers: So the root operator can confirm the file was not altered in transit
It encrypts the request
The configuration wizard requires it to continue
quizzes.explanation: An independently recorded hash lets the ceremony verify integrity. It does not encrypt anything — it proves the same file arrived.

quizzes.question: The new issuing CA is waiting with its service stopped. What is correct?
answers: Reinstall the role until the service starts
That is the expected state until the signed certificate is installed
Join the root to the domain to finish the setup
quizzes.explanation: A subordinate CA cannot run before its CA certificate exists. The waiting state is normal, not a failure to fix.

recap: The issuing host has its final name, addressing, DNS, and time before the role install.
The request file carries the public key only.
The request’s fields and hash are reviewed and recorded before transfer.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 walks the request through the offline signing ceremony.

lessons.title: Sign through the offline ceremony
lessons.summary: A signing ceremony connects an approved request to an approved CA identity. A matching filename alone is not proof that the root should trust the request.
steps: Use approved removable media and custody procedures to bring the request to the root. Recalculate its hash and compare it with the independently recorded value; inspect the request before submission.

Verify the root's issued-certificate validity policy and publication extensions. In Certification Authority, submit the request, review its pending entry, and issue it only after the required approval.

Export the subordinate certificate, root certificate, and current root CRL. Check identities, constraints, validity, signatures, URLs, and revocation data against the approved hierarchy. Record file hashes and the request ID.

Transfer only the approved public artifacts back to the connected environment. Match published filenames to the URLs embedded in certificates, retain the ceremony record and protected backup, then shut down and secure the root.
lessons.command:
# Inspect public artifacts; use your actual approved paths.
certutil -dump C:\CAConfig\IssuingCA.cer
certutil -dump C:\CAConfig\RootCA.crl
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\CAConfig\IssuingCA.cer, C:\CAConfig\RootCA.cer, C:\CAConfig\RootCA.crl
lessons.check: Artifact identities, signatures, validity, and custody checks pass. The root remains offline; a field dump alone is not end-to-end trust validation.
lessons.evidence: Keep approval, request ID, artifact hashes, verified certificate/CRL properties, media custody, and root shutdown evidence together.

model.label: Offline trust, step 2
model.text: The ceremony you perform in this lesson, shown as a custody walk with no network link to the root.

objectives: Verify request integrity at the root before submission.
Issue the subordinate certificate under the approved validity policy.
Export and verify the public artifacts, then return the root to a secured state.

quizzes.question: Which transfer preserves the root boundary?
answers: An automated shared folder on the root
Approved removable media carrying the reviewed request and public artifacts
Temporary direct internet access
quizzes.explanation: This training architecture uses manual, human-controlled transfer. It never adds a live link to the root.

quizzes.question: What leaves the root environment after the ceremony?
answers: The root’s private-key backup
A live network share for future requests
Only approved public artifacts: the subordinate certificate, root certificate, and current CRL
quizzes.explanation: The boundary stays intact: public artifacts travel on approved media; keys and live connections never do.

quizzes.question: The request’s recalculated hash does not match the recorded value. What now?
answers: Stop and investigate; do not submit the request
Submit it anyway and compare afterward
Regenerate the hash until it matches
quizzes.explanation: A hash mismatch means the file is not the one that was approved. Submitting it would sign an unverified request.

recap: Integrity is verified before submission, and issuance follows explicit approval.
Artifact identities, validity, and URLs are checked against the plan.
The ceremony record, hashes, and root shutdown are all evidence.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 brings the issuing CA online and publishes the trust data.

lessons.title: Activate issuance and publish trust data
lessons.summary: A running CA is only one part of a working PKI. Clients also need the approved trust anchor, the intermediate certificate, and current revocation information at the advertised locations.
steps: Verify the returned artifacts and import the approved root certificate into the issuing server's trusted root store. Complete CA certificate installation through Certification Authority and start Certificate Services.

Configure the issuing CA's AIA/CDP settings before issuing test certificates. Publish current root and issuing certificates and CRLs to the planned internal locations, preserving the actual filenames referenced by their extensions.

Distribute the approved root trust through the managed domain policy and arrange the required intermediate/directory publication with delegated administrators. Public CA certificates and CRLs may be readable to clients; private keys and backups must never enter that web directory.

Publish only the certificate templates required for the lab. Review purpose, subject construction, key settings, validity, and enrollment permissions; grant a small test group the minimum enrollment rights first.
lessons.command:
# Inspect the issuing CA after installation and publication.
Get-Service CertSvc
certutil -getreg CA\CRLPublicationURLs
certutil -getreg CA\CACertPublicationURLs
certutil -store Root
certutil -store CA
lessons.check: Issuance is configured, the approved trust chain reaches the client, and the exact published URLs return the current files from the internal network.
lessons.evidence: Keep publication mappings, permissions, template settings, trust-distribution policy, and retrieval results.
objectives: Install the signed certificate and start Certificate Services.
Publish certificates and CRLs at the exact advertised URLs.
Publish only the certificate templates the lab requires.

quizzes.question: Which files belong in the client-readable PKI publication directory?
answers: Root and issuing private-key backups
Administrator passwords and recovery keys
Approved public CA certificates and CRLs
quizzes.explanation: Clients need public trust and revocation artifacts. Publication must not expose CA secrets or recovery material.

quizzes.question: Why must published filenames match the URLs embedded in certificates?
answers: The CA service will not start otherwise
Clients fetch exactly those URLs; a renamed file breaks chain building and revocation checks
Filenames control template permissions
quizzes.explanation: Chain building and revocation checking follow the embedded AIA and CDP URLs literally. Publication must serve those names.

quizzes.question: How does the approved root certificate reach domain clients?
answers: Each user imports it manually from email
It replicates automatically through DNS
Through the managed domain policy trust distribution
quizzes.explanation: Group Policy distributes the trusted root deliberately and reversibly, which keeps trust decisions managed.

recap: The trust chain and current CRLs are reachable at the advertised internal URLs.
Root trust distributes through managed domain policy.
Only required templates are published, with minimal enrollment rights.
lessons.next: The final lesson validates the whole system from a client’s point of view.

lessons.title: Validate enrollment, revocation, and recovery
lessons.summary: Finish from a clean domain client. Verify the experience of a relying system, including what happens when a certificate is no longer trusted.
steps: Enroll a disposable test certificate using the approved template. Export only its public certificate as test.cer and inspect the subject, purpose, issuer, and validity.

On a clean validation client, verify the chain and retrieval using the command below. Inspect each AIA/CDP URL and current CRL dates; cached success is insufficient evidence of publication reachability.

Revoke only the disposable test certificate, publish an updated issuing CRL, and verify that a fresh client evaluation detects revocation. Diagnose retrieval or stale-publication problems rather than turning off revocation checks.

Record owners and reminders for root/issuing CRL publication, certificate renewal, backup, and an isolated recovery rehearsal. Schedule offline root ceremonies early enough to transfer and publish replacement CRLs before expiry.
lessons.command:
# On the validation client; test.cer is the disposable public certificate.
certutil -dump test.cer
certutil -urlfetch -verify test.cer
lessons.check: A valid test certificate chains to the approved root and retrieves current revocation data. After revocation and publication, the test certificate is rejected for the expected reason.
lessons.evidence: Finish the PKI checklist with enrollment, retrieval and revocation results, renewal dates, backup verification, and recovery ownership.

model.label: Use a web app, step 2
model.text: A browser checks the server certificate against the internal chain you just validated.

objectives: Enroll and inspect a disposable test certificate.
Verify chain building and revocation retrieval from a clean client.
Prove revocation works, and schedule the renewals that keep the PKI alive.

quizzes.question: A valid certificate fails because its CRL cannot be retrieved. What is the next step?
answers: Fix and retest the publication or reachability problem
Disable revocation checking for all clients
Copy the root private key to the client
quizzes.explanation: Reliable revocation publication is part of the service. Bypassing the check conceals the failed dependency.

quizzes.question: What does certutil -urlfetch -verify prove that a plain certificate inspection does not?
answers: That the private key is backed up
That the AIA and CDP URLs are reachable and return current data
That the root is still offline
quizzes.explanation: The -urlfetch option follows the embedded URLs live, exposing publication or reachability failures that cached checks hide.

quizzes.question: Why schedule offline root ceremonies ahead of CRL expiry?
answers: A replacement CRL must be transferred and published before the old one expires
The root certificate expires monthly
Clients delete their trust store on expiry
quizzes.explanation: If the root CRL lapses, revocation checking fails across the hierarchy. Manual transfer takes lead time, so it is scheduled early.

recap: A clean client builds the chain and retrieves live revocation data.
A revoked test certificate is rejected for the expected reason.
Renewal, backup, and recovery each have an owner and a date.
lessons.next: That completes Configure a Root CA & issuing CA. Course 1.5 connects and segments the network, and course 1.6 then finishes the PKI services: the pki.sbd.test publication site and template administration.

prerequisites: Complete the identity build and DNS courses with replication and name resolution verified on both controllers.
Use the isolated Windows Server 2025 environment and an account approved for organizational unit and Group Policy administration.
Have an approved connected system and removable-media procedure for bringing downloaded hardening content into the lab.
labNote: This course designs the organizational unit (OU) structure, applies the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) Group Policy package, and verifies the result with Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) scans. Paths, versions, and session locations below are examples — adapt them to your tooling. Expect STIG settings to change behavior: that is the point, and the reason everything is scanned and recorded.

sources.title: Microsoft · Redirect the Users and Computers containers
Microsoft · Create and manage the Group Policy Central Store
Microsoft · What's new in Windows Server 2025
DISA · STIG Group Policy Objects package
DISA · SRG/STIG tools (SCC and STIG Viewer)

lessons.title: Design and build the OU structure
lessons.summary: Organizational units exist for delegation and Group Policy targeting, not to mirror an org chart. Build the structure the hardening policies will hang on before importing any of them.
objectives: Design an OU structure around delegation and Group Policy targeting.
Create protected OUs and redirect the default Computers and Users containers.
Explain why the built-in Domain Controllers OU stays untouched.
steps: Design the structure by administration: a top-level SBD OU containing Servers, Workstations, Users, Groups, and an Admin OU for privileged accounts. The built-in Domain Controllers OU stays where it is and keeps its name.
Create the planned OUs with accidental-deletion protection enabled. Record each OU's purpose and who will administer its contents; an OU with no delegation or policy purpose is clutter.

Redirect the default Computers and Users containers to managed OUs with redircmp and redirusr. Group Policy cannot be linked to the default containers, so anything landing there would get only domain-level policy, never the OU-linked hardening.

Keep privileged accounts and systems separate: the Admin OU holds the identities that administer domain controllers. The issuing CA from course 1.4 joins the Servers OU for now; course 1.7 gives Tier 0 servers their own OU. Do not nest deeper than the delegation plan requires.
lessons.command:
Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter * | Select-Object Name, DistinguishedName
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object ComputersContainer, UsersContainer
(Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Identity 'OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Properties ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion).ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion
lessons.check: The planned OUs exist with deletion protection, the default container redirects point at managed OUs, and each OU has a recorded purpose and administrator.
lessons.evidence: Keep the OU design sheet: each OU's distinguished name, purpose, delegated administrator, and the redirect commands with their output.

quizzes.question: What should drive the shape of the OU structure?
answers: Group Policy targeting and delegated administration
The company org chart
Alphabetical order of departments
quizzes.explanation: OUs are an administrative tool. Policy and delegation boundaries define them; reporting lines belong in HR systems.

quizzes.question: Why redirect the default Computers container?
answers: It makes domain join faster
Group Policy cannot be linked to the default containers, so new machines would miss the OU-linked hardening
It is required before DNS works
quizzes.explanation: Redirection sends newly joined machines into an OU where policy applies from their first start.

quizzes.question: Where do the two domain controllers live after this lesson?
answers: In the new Servers OU
In the built-in Domain Controllers OU, unchanged
In the Users container
quizzes.explanation: Domain controllers stay in their built-in OU — it is where the DC hardening policies link in lesson 4.

recap: OUs follow administration, not the org chart.
The default containers are redirected so nothing joins unmanaged.
The Domain Controllers OU remains the link point for DC policies.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 brings the DISA tooling across the air gap the same controlled way course 1.4 will later carry certificate requests.

lessons.title: Stage the tooling across the air gap
lessons.summary: The hardening content is downloaded artifacts: the DISA Group Policy object (GPO) package, the SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC), and STIG Viewer. They cross the boundary the way everything does here — reviewed, hashed, and carried on approved removable media.
objectives: Identify the DISA artifacts the hardening work needs.
Move downloaded tooling across the air gap with hash verification.
Record versions so scans stay comparable over time.
steps: On an approved connected system, download the current DISA GPO package and the SRG/STIG tools (SCC and STIG Viewer) from DISA's public site. Note each file's version and the quarterly release it belongs to.
Record a SHA-256 hash for every file on the connected side, then transfer the set with the approved removable-media procedure. No live link to the lab is created for convenience.
In the lab, recalculate and compare every hash before opening anything. A mismatch stops the work, exactly as it would in the PKI signing ceremony.

Install SCC and STIG Viewer on an administrative host and stage the GPO package where the import lesson can reach it. Record tool versions; scan results are only comparable when the benchmark and tool versions are known.
lessons.command:
Get-ChildItem C:\Staging\DISA | Select-Object Name, Length
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Staging\DISA\*
lessons.check: Every transferred file's hash matches the value recorded on the connected side, and tool and package versions are written down.
lessons.evidence: Keep the transfer record: file names, versions, both hash sets, media custody, and the date.

quizzes.question: Why hash the files on both sides of the transfer?
answers: To prove the same files arrived unaltered
To compress them for the media
Because SCC refuses unhashed input
quizzes.explanation: An independently recorded hash is how a human-controlled transfer proves integrity across the boundary.

quizzes.question: Which release cadence do the DISA GPO package and STIGs follow?
answers: Weekly
Quarterly
Only at new Windows releases
quizzes.explanation: DISA refreshes STIG content on a quarterly cycle, which this course's standing rescan cadence follows.

quizzes.question: A hash mismatch appears on the lab side. What now?
answers: Open the file and inspect it manually
Stop, set the media aside, and repeat the approved transfer
Regenerate hashes until they match
quizzes.explanation: A mismatch means the file is not the one that was reviewed. Unverified content never gets opened inside the boundary.

recap: The GPO package, SCC, and STIG Viewer come from DISA's public site.
Hashes are recorded on both sides of the boundary.
Tool and package versions are part of the evidence.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 measures the network before anything is hardened.

lessons.title: Capture the pre-hardening baseline
lessons.summary: Measure before you change. A scan of the freshly built controllers shows the honest starting point, teaches what the operating system already secures by default, and becomes the before picture every later scan is compared against.
objectives: Run a SCAP baseline scan against both domain controllers.
Distinguish automated results from manual-review items.
Preserve raw results as evidence with hashes and versions.
steps: On each domain controller, run SCC with the Windows Server 2025 STIG benchmark and the directory-related content staged for this course. Save each session's results with the host name and date.

Open the results and read, don't just count. Note which checks already pass: Windows Server 2025 ships with defaults such as required signing on outbound SMB connections and LDAP sealing on new deployments, so part of the STIG is green before you touch anything.
Separate the automated results from the manual checks. SCAP answers what a scanner can read; items marked for manual review go to STIG Viewer for a human answer in lesson 5.
Store the raw result files unmodified, with recorded hashes. The baseline is evidence; a cleaned-up copy is a summary, not the record.
lessons.command:
# Adapt paths to your SCC installation and session directory.
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\baseline -Recurse -Include *.xml | Select-Object Name, LastWriteTime
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\baseline\*
lessons.check: Both controllers have a dated baseline result set, the already-compliant OS defaults are noted, and the raw files are hashed and stored.
lessons.evidence: Keep the per-host result files, their hashes, the benchmark and tool versions, and a short note of what the OS defaults already covered.

quizzes.question: Why scan before applying any GPO?
answers: The scanner requires an unhardened system
A dated before record makes every later change measurable and attributable
Scanning after GPOs is not possible
quizzes.explanation: The baseline is the comparison point. Without it, the rescan proves only a state, not what your hardening changed.

quizzes.question: Several checks pass before any hardening. What is the likely reason on Windows Server 2025?
answers: The scanner is misconfigured
Earlier lessons secretly applied GPOs
The OS ships secure defaults, such as required SMB signing, that satisfy those checks
quizzes.explanation: Windows Server 2025 raised several security defaults, so a fresh build already meets part of the benchmark.

quizzes.question: What happens with checks the scanner marks for manual review?
answers: They are ignored as not applicable
They count as failures forever
A person answers them in STIG Viewer with recorded rationale
quizzes.explanation: SCAP automates what a scanner can read; manual checks need a reviewer's observed evidence to be defensible.

recap: The baseline is measured, dated, and stored unmodified.
Secure-by-default items are recognized, not claimed as your work.
Manual checks are queued for human review.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 applies the DISA policies that close the gap you just measured.

lessons.title: Import and link the DISA GPOs
lessons.summary: Group Policy is how the STIG becomes configuration. Import the package into the central store, link by organizational unit, and keep the lab's deliberate deviations written down rather than silently skipped.
objectives: Stage the package's templates in the Group Policy central store.
Import DISA's policies and link them by organizational unit.
Handle lab-specific deviations with documentation instead of silent edits.
steps: Copy the package's ADMX and ADML templates into the domain's Group Policy central store (the PolicyDefinitions folder in SYSVOL) so every editor on any domain controller shows the same settings.

Create empty GPOs named for the package's policies and import the package's settings into them with the GPMC Import Settings wizard or Import-GPO. Keep DISA's names with a local prefix so the source release stays identifiable.

Link the domain-controller policies to the Domain Controllers OU and the member-server policies to the Servers OU for future systems. Review link order and inheritance; do not use Enforced as a shortcut around understanding precedence.

Walk the settings that need a decision in this network — anything referencing infrastructure the lab does not have. Record each deviation with its rationale instead of deleting the setting, then update policy and confirm application.
lessons.command:
Get-ChildItem \\sbd.test\SYSVOL\sbd.test\Policies\PolicyDefinitions | Measure-Object
Get-GPO -All | Select-Object DisplayName, GpoStatus, ModificationTime
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Domain Controllers,DC=sbd,DC=test'
gpupdate /force
gpresult /r /scope:computer
lessons.check: The central store serves the package's templates, the imported GPOs are linked to the intended OUs, gpresult shows them applying, and every deviation has a written reason.
lessons.evidence: Keep the import record: package release, GPO names and links, inheritance output, and the deviation list with rationale and owner.

model.label: Sign in, step 4
model.text: After sign-in, members read Group Policy over LDAP and SMB from SYSVOL. That is how the GPOs you link reach every machine.

quizzes.question: Why does the OU work from lesson 1 matter here?
answers: GPOs link to OUs, so the structure decides which systems receive which hardening
OUs make the GPO files smaller
DISA requires an OU named DISA
quizzes.explanation: Policy targeting is the OU structure's whole job: domain-controller policies to the Domain Controllers OU, server policies to the Servers OU.

quizzes.question: Where do the ADMX templates go so every domain controller's editor agrees?
answers: Each administrator's desktop
The Group Policy central store in SYSVOL
The offline root CA
quizzes.explanation: The central store replicates with SYSVOL, so every Group Policy editor in the domain reads the same definitions.

quizzes.question: A STIG setting assumes infrastructure the lab doesn't have. What is the right move?
answers: Delete the setting from the GPO quietly
Mark the whole package not applicable
Record a deviation with rationale and keep it visible for the assessment
quizzes.explanation: Documented deviations keep the hardening honest. A silent edit hides a decision an assessor will later need to see.

recap: The central store keeps policy definitions consistent across controllers.
Links follow the OU design; precedence is understood, not forced.
Deviations are documented decisions, not deletions.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 proves what the policies changed.

lessons.title: Rescan, reconcile, and record
lessons.summary: The second scan is the verdict. Compare it with the baseline, let the automated results fill the checklists, and give every remaining open item a human answer.
objectives: Re-scan with matched benchmark and tool versions and compare against the baseline.
Populate checklists from scan results and answer manual checks with evidence.
Classify every remaining open item explicitly.
steps: Rerun SCC on both controllers with the same benchmark and tool versions as the baseline. Changing versions between scans makes the comparison meaningless.
Compare the two result sets per host: which checks moved from open to compliant, which stayed open, and whether anything regressed. Attribute each change to the policy that caused it.
Create the course checklists in STIG Viewer and bring in the scan results so automated passes are populated. Work the manual-review items one by one, recording the observed evidence for each answer.

Classify what remains open: a finding to fix now, a documented deviation from lesson 4, or a candidate for a Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) — the artifact the Body of Evidence course teaches you to write.
lessons.command:
# Compare result sets; adapt paths to your evidence layout.
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\baseline, C:\Evidence\hardened -Recurse -Include *.xml | Select-Object Directory, Name
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\hardened\*
gpresult /h C:\Evidence\hardened\SBD-DC01-gpresult.html
lessons.check: Both hosts show the expected movement from the baseline, every change is attributable, and every open item is a finding, a deviation, or a POA&M candidate — never unexplained.
lessons.evidence: Keep the before/after comparison, the populated checklist files, manual-check answers with their observed evidence, and the classification of remaining opens.

quizzes.question: Why keep the same benchmark and SCC versions for the rescan?
answers: Newer versions cost more
Results are only comparable when the measuring stick didn't change
DISA forbids upgrading mid-quarter
quizzes.explanation: A version change alters which checks exist and how they evaluate, so the before/after comparison would mix causes.

quizzes.question: A check is still open and the lab intends to leave it that way, with a reason. What is that called?
answers: A false positive
A passing result
A documented deviation — and possibly, later, a POA&M entry
quizzes.explanation: An intentional, justified open item is a deviation; one that will be fixed on a plan becomes a POA&M entry in the authorization path.

quizzes.question: What makes a checklist entry for a manual check defensible?
answers: The reviewer's observed evidence and rationale are recorded with it
The box is checked
It was green in the automated scan
quizzes.explanation: A manual answer without recorded evidence is an assertion. The observation is what an assessor can verify.

recap: Same versions, honest comparison.
Automated results fill the checklist; humans answer the rest.
Open items end the lesson classified, never mysterious.
lessons.next: The final lesson turns this into a standing practice with owners and triggers.

lessons.title: Set the rescan cadence and exception record
lessons.summary: Hardening is a state you maintain, not a step you finish. Close the course by deciding who rescans, when, and which event forces an early look.
objectives: Consolidate deviations into an owned, dated exception record.
Define the quarterly and event-driven rescan cadence.
Export and back up the applied policy state as evidence.
steps: Consolidate the deviation records into one exception list: setting, reason, risk note, owner, and review date. This list travels into the authorization path as part of the Body of Evidence.

Set the standing cadence: review each quarterly DISA release for applicable updates, and rescan after any role addition or significant configuration change. Course 1.5's closing delta scan is the first scheduled instance, and course 1.6 scans the PKI servers the same way.
Export the Group Policy reports and back up the GPO set so the applied policy state is recoverable and reviewable without a live console.
Write the handoff note a future administrator or assessor would need: where the evidence lives, which versions produced it, and what is intentionally open.
lessons.command:
Get-GPOReport -All -ReportType Html -Path C:\Evidence\gpo-report.html
Backup-GPO -All -Path C:\Evidence\gpo-backup
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\gpo-report.html
lessons.check: The exception list has owners and review dates, the GPO set is exported and backed up, and the rescan triggers are written where the next course will meet them.
lessons.evidence: Finish the hardening checklist: exception list, GPO backup location, report hashes, the cadence, and the named owner of the next review.

quizzes.question: What triggers a rescan before the next quarterly cycle?
answers: Only a calendar reminder
A role addition or significant configuration change
Nothing — quarterly is the only trigger
quizzes.explanation: Change is the other trigger. Course 1.5 ends with exactly such a delta scan, and so do the build courses after it.

quizzes.question: Why back up the GPO set as part of the evidence?
answers: It makes gpupdate run faster
DISA requires backups inside SYSVOL
The applied policy state becomes recoverable and reviewable, independent of a live console
quizzes.explanation: A backup plus reports lets anyone — including a future you — verify or restore the applied state without trusting memory.

quizzes.question: Where does the exception list end up in the bigger arc?
answers: It is deleted after the course
In the Body of Evidence the authorization path organizes and assesses
Inside the offline root CA
quizzes.explanation: Deviations and POA&M candidates are authorization-package material; course 2.2 shows how artifacts like this list join the Body of Evidence.

recap: Exceptions have owners and review dates.
Rescans follow the DISA quarter and every meaningful change.
The applied GPO state is exported, backed up, and hashed.
lessons.next: That completes hardening the baseline. Course 1.4 builds the two-tier PKI on this hardened base, and course 1.5 runs this cadence's first delta scan.

prerequisites: Complete courses 1.1–1.4: verified domain controllers, DNS, the hardened baseline with its scan cadence, and the two-tier PKI.
Provision a new virtual machine for the layer-3 router (SBD-CORE01 in this sample) with one interface per VLAN, and a Windows Server 2025 VM for SBD-TIME01 at 10.0.20.40.
Have the Inside the Network VLAN plan at hand: VLANs 10–80 on 10.0.X.0/24 subnets plus management VLAN 100 for network devices, with .1 reserved as each gateway in this sample.
labNote: This course connects the eight VLANs through a router the lab controls, enforces default-deny between them with a documented exception register, and stands up the internal time service. The router platform is your choice — the lessons describe what to configure and verify every result from the Windows side, so the checks work whatever appliance you pick. The network still has no path across the air gap.

sources.title: Microsoft · Configure a firewall for Active Directory domains
Microsoft · Windows Time service tools and settings

lessons.title: Design the segmentation and service paths
lessons.summary: A VLAN is a boundary only if something enforces it. Before touching the router, write the policy: default deny between VLANs, and an exception register where every permitted path names its source, destination, port, and reason.
objectives: Translate the Inside the Network VLAN plan into a default-deny segmentation policy.
Draft the access control list (ACL) exception register from the documented service paths.
Record the gateway addressing and routing decisions before any device is built.
steps: List the eight VLANs with their subnets and purposes from the network plan. Reserve .1 in each subnet as the gateway for this sample, and record that no route crosses the air-gapped boundary.
Write the policy sentence first: traffic between VLANs is denied unless a register entry permits it. Segmentation alone does not establish enforcement — the access control lists do.

Draft the register's first entries from paths the built systems already need: every VLAN to the domain controllers for DNS, Kerberos, LDAP, SMB, RPC, and time (UDP 123), because domain members take their time from the domain controllers; SBD-DC01, the primary domain controller (PDC) emulator, to SBD-TIME01 — the only system that syncs from the reference clock; and the admin VLAN to the tiers it manages. One row per path: source, destination, service and port, justification, owner.
Mark the paths that do not exist yet (workstation pools, business services) as planned rows, and decide the change process: who may add a register entry, and what evidence each addition needs.
lessons.command:
# Record the pre-routing state on each DC — today there is no gateway.
Get-NetIPConfiguration
Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 | Select-Object DestinationPrefix, NextHop | Sort-Object DestinationPrefix -Unique
lessons.check: The register exists with every current path justified, the gateway plan is written, and the pre-routing state of both DCs is captured as the before picture.
lessons.evidence: Keep the segmentation policy statement, the exception register with owners, and the captured pre-routing output.

model.label: the network topology
model.text: Each VLAN is a platform around the core switch, floating over the building, so you can check your segment plan against the design and see where each system physically lives.

quizzes.question: What makes a VLAN an enforced boundary?
answers: The VLAN number itself
The access control lists that deny traffic between VLANs by default
Giving each VLAN a different color in the diagram
quizzes.explanation: Segmentation describes the layout; the ACLs are the enforcement. Without them, routing simply connects everything.

quizzes.question: What belongs in every exception register row?
answers: Source, destination, service and port, justification, and an owner
Only the port number
The VLAN colors
quizzes.explanation: A permitted path without a recorded reason and owner cannot be defended at assessment time — or safely removed later.

quizzes.question: Why capture the DCs' routing state before the router exists?
answers: The output configures the router automatically
Routing cannot be inspected after a gateway is set
It is the before picture that makes the connectivity change measurable
quizzes.explanation: The same before-and-after habit as the hardening course: record the starting state so the change itself becomes evidence.

recap: Default deny between VLANs; the register holds the exceptions.
Every permitted path has a source, destination, port, reason, and owner.
Gateways are planned (.1 per subnet) and the air gap stays unrouted.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 builds the router that will enforce this design.

lessons.title: Build the core router
lessons.summary: The core is a virtual machine the lab controls: one interface per VLAN, the planned gateway address on each, and no default route anywhere — there is nowhere outside this network to go.
objectives: Deploy the layer-3 router VM with an interface in every VLAN.
Assign the planned gateway addresses with routing enabled and no external route.
Point the built systems at their gateways and prove basic reachability.
steps: Create the router VM (SBD-CORE01 in this sample) with one virtual interface attached to each of the eight VLAN networks. Record the platform and version you chose; the register, not the vendor syntax, is the course's deliverable.

Assign each interface its subnet's .1 address and enable routing between the interfaces. Do not configure a default route or any path toward the hypervisor's outside networks — the air gap is a routing decision too.
Set the gateway on the built systems: 10.0.10.1 on both domain controllers and 10.0.30.1 on the issuing CA. The offline root gets nothing; it stays off the network entirely.

From a host in another VLAN, prove the route: reach each gateway, then a DC address. Leave the ACLs permissive for this one lesson so routing and filtering failures cannot be confused — lesson 3 locks it down.
lessons.command:
Get-NetIPConfiguration | Select-Object InterfaceAlias, IPv4Address, IPv4DefaultGateway
Test-NetConnection 10.0.10.1
Test-NetConnection 10.0.10.10 -TraceRoute
lessons.check: Each built system shows its planned gateway, the trace crosses the router in one hop, and the router holds no route toward anything outside the lab.
lessons.evidence: Record the router platform and version, its interface and address table, the gateway changes on each system, and the trace output.

quizzes.question: Why does the router get no default route?
answers: Default routes are slower
The network is air-gapped — a route toward the outside would quietly break that boundary
Routers cannot hold more than eight routes
quizzes.explanation: The air gap is maintained in configuration as much as in cabling. A default route toward the hypervisor's networks would undo it.

quizzes.question: Why leave ACLs permissive during this one lesson?
answers: ACLs are optional in a lab
So a failed test clearly means a routing problem, not a filtering decision
The register is written later
quizzes.explanation: Changing one layer at a time keeps faults attributable — the same discipline as the DNS troubleshooting lesson.

quizzes.question: Which system never receives a gateway?
answers: SBD-DC02
SBD-SUBCA01
SBD-ROOTCA01 — the offline root stays off the network
quizzes.explanation: The root's protection is having no network path at all. Routing reaches it never, by design.

recap: One router interface per VLAN, .1 as each gateway, routing on.
No default route — the air gap survives in the routing table.
Reachability is proven before any filtering begins.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 turns the register into enforced access control lists.

lessons.title: Enforce default-deny with the register
lessons.summary: Now the policy becomes configuration: deny between VLANs by default, permit exactly the register's rows, and log what gets dropped so the denials are visible evidence, not silence.
objectives: Implement default-deny filtering between all VLANs.
Permit the Active Directory, PKI, and time service paths from the register.
Log denied traffic so enforcement produces evidence.
steps: Apply the inter-VLAN default-deny rule on the router, with logging for denied packets. The log of what was blocked is as much evidence as the list of what was allowed.

Permit the directory paths from every VLAN to VLAN 10 per Microsoft's Active Directory port documentation: DNS (53), Kerberos (88 and 464), LDAP (389/636), global catalog (3268/3269), SMB (445), and the RPC endpoint mapper with its dynamic range — the register row for RPC should name the range decision explicitly.

Permit time the way Windows Time actually flows: UDP 123 from every VLAN to both domain controllers, and UDP 123 from SBD-DC01 alone to SBD-TIME01. Permit HTTP to the pki.sbd.test publication service in VLAN 30 so clients can fetch certificates and revocation lists.

Record the VLAN 80 peer denies now — workstation-to-workstation SMB and Remote Desktop — as host-firewall rows: traffic inside one VLAN never reaches the router, so course 1.9 enforces them with each PC's own firewall. Then read back the full rule set against the register line by line — anything configured but not registered gets removed or registered, never ignored.
lessons.command:
# From a test host outside VLAN 10: permitted paths answer, everything else fails.
Test-NetConnection SBD-DC01.sbd.test -Port 53
Test-NetConnection SBD-DC01.sbd.test -Port 88
Test-NetConnection SBD-DC01.sbd.test -Port 389
Test-NetConnection 10.0.10.10 -Port 3389   # expected: TcpTestSucceeded False
lessons.check: Registered paths succeed, an unregistered port fails and appears in the router's deny log, and the rule set matches the register with no unexplained entries in either direction.
lessons.evidence: Keep the exported rule set, the register cross-check, the permitted-path test output, and a captured deny-log entry for the blocked test.

model.label: What if a PC tries SQL?
model.text: Default deny at the core stops a workstation from reaching the database directly.

quizzes.question: A rule exists on the router but not in the register. What happens?
answers: It stays — the router is authoritative
It is removed or registered with justification; configuration and register must agree
It is ignored until the next quarter
quizzes.explanation: The register is the authority an assessor reads. Configuration that drifted from it is either undocumented access or dead weight.

quizzes.question: Why log denied traffic?
answers: Denials are evidence that enforcement works, and the first clue when a legitimate path was missed
Logs make the router faster
Logging is only required on port 3389
quizzes.explanation: A silent deny proves nothing and hides mistakes. The log turns the boundary into something you can demonstrate.

quizzes.question: Which port set does a domain member need to reach the DCs?
answers: Only ICMP
Just port 80
DNS, Kerberos, LDAP, global catalog, SMB, and RPC — the documented AD port set
quizzes.explanation: Active Directory is several cooperating services. Microsoft's firewall documentation lists the ports a member actually uses.

recap: Default deny is in force; the register's rows are the only openings.
Denied traffic is logged — enforcement you can show, not assume.
Rule set and register reconcile exactly, both directions.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 gives the network its clock.

lessons.title: Stand up SBD-TIME01 and the time hierarchy
lessons.summary: Kerberos tolerates minutes of skew, not more, and an air-gapped network has no internet time to lean on. Build the internal reference, point the PDC emulator at it, and let the domain hierarchy carry time to everything else.
objectives: Configure SBD-TIME01 as the lab's internal reference clock.
Point the PDC emulator at it and keep the rest on the domain hierarchy.
Document the accuracy, fallback, and drift decisions the model calls for.
steps: Build SBD-TIME01 at 10.0.20.40 as a workgroup or domain-joined Windows Server 2025 host with the Windows Time service configured as an NTP server. In an air-gapped lab its clock is the reference by declaration — record the source decision (host clock, or an approved hardware source) with its expected accuracy and drift threshold.

On SBD-DC01, the domain controller holding the PDC emulator role, configure Windows Time to use SBD-TIME01 as its manual peer and mark it reliable. Only the PDC emulator points at TIME01: SBD-DC02 syncs from the PDC emulator, every other domain member keeps the default domain-hierarchy sync from the domain controllers, and the domain-joined Linux servers in later courses point chrony or ntpd at both domain controllers.

Confirm the register's time rows are active — members to both domain controllers on UDP 123, and SBD-DC01 alone to SBD-TIME01 — and that the hardening Group Policy objects (GPOs) from course 1.3 do not conflict with the time settings. If a Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) value and this design disagree, the deviation record from that course is where the decision lives.
Verify the chain end to end: TIME01 serving, the PDC emulator sourcing from it, SBD-DC02 and a member server sourcing from a domain controller, and offsets within your recorded threshold.
lessons.command:
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object PDCEmulator   # expected: SBD-DC01.sbd.test
# On the PDC emulator, then on SBD-DC02 and a member server:
w32tm /query /source
w32tm /query /status
w32tm /stripchart /computer:10.0.20.40 /samples:3 /dataonly   # from SBD-DC01 only
lessons.check: The PDC emulator reports SBD-TIME01 as its source, SBD-DC02 and the member server report a domain controller, and measured offsets sit inside the documented threshold.
lessons.evidence: Record the time design decisions, the source and status output from both controllers and the member, the stripchart offsets, and the register rows that permit time: members to the domain controllers, and SBD-DC01 to SBD-TIME01.

model.label: SBD-TIME01
model.text: The time server, its address, and every rule in the register that names it.

quizzes.question: Which system syncs directly with SBD-TIME01?
answers: Every domain member individually
The domain controller holding the PDC emulator role
Only the offline root CA
quizzes.explanation: The PDC emulator is the domain's time authority; everything else follows the domain hierarchy from there.

quizzes.question: What does the air gap change about time design?
answers: Nothing — pool.ntp.org still works
Kerberos stops needing accurate time
There is no internet source, so the internal reference and its drift threshold are documented decisions
quizzes.explanation: With no external source, accuracy is whatever the lab declares and monitors — which is why the model tags this host AU-8 and SC-45.

quizzes.question: Why does time matter to authentication at all?
answers: Kerberos rejects tickets outside its allowed clock skew, so drifting clocks become sign-in failures
DNS records expire hourly
Passwords change with the clock
quizzes.explanation: Kerberos builds replay protection on timestamps. Skew beyond the tolerance breaks authentication before anything looks wrong.

quizzes.question: Where does a domain workstation get its time in this design?
answers: From SBD-TIME01 directly
From a domain controller over UDP 123, following the domain hierarchy
From the core router
quizzes.explanation: Windows Time follows the domain hierarchy: members sync from a domain controller, the other domain controller from the PDC emulator, and only the PDC emulator from SBD-TIME01. That is why the register permits UDP 123 from every VLAN to the domain controllers, not to SBD-TIME01.

recap: TIME01 is the declared reference; its accuracy decisions are written down.
Only the PDC emulator peers with it; the hierarchy carries the rest.
Offsets are measured and inside the threshold, not assumed.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 proves the whole boundary — what passes, what fails, and that both are intended.

lessons.title: Prove the paths and the denials
lessons.summary: A segmented network is proven twice: every registered path works from where it is supposed to work, and the paths you never granted fail — visibly, in the log.
objectives: Test the permitted-path matrix from each VLAN against the register.
Prove representative denials and capture their log entries.
Confirm the directory still behaves correctly across the routed network.
steps: From a test host in each populated VLAN, run the register's permitted paths as a scripted matrix: directory ports and time to VLAN 10, and HTTP to pki.sbd.test. Record source VLAN, destination, port, and result for every row.

Run the deliberate failures: a port no register row permits, from a VLAN that should not reach it — for example, time straight to SBD-TIME01 from a test host outside VLAN 20, since only SBD-DC01 may reach it. Confirm the failure and find its entry in the router's deny log — the pair is the evidence.
Re-run the course 1.2 and 1.4 verification habits across the boundary: resolve the domain SRV records and fetch pki.sbd.test's certificate revocation list from outside VLANs 10 and 30.
File the matrix and the deny-log captures with the register. Any mismatch — a registered path failing or an unregistered path passing — is a finding to resolve before the course ends, not a note.
lessons.command:
$targets = @(@('SBD-DC01.sbd.test',53),@('SBD-DC01.sbd.test',88),@('SBD-DC01.sbd.test',389),@('pki.sbd.test',80))
foreach ($t in $targets) { Test-NetConnection $t[0] -Port $t[1] | Select-Object ComputerName, RemotePort, TcpTestSucceeded }
w32tm /stripchart /computer:SBD-DC01.sbd.test /samples:3 /dataonly   # time over UDP 123 answers
w32tm /stripchart /computer:10.0.20.40 /samples:1 /dataonly   # from a test host outside VLAN 20: expected to fail (only SBD-DC01 may reach TIME01)
Resolve-DnsName _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.sbd.test -Type SRV
lessons.check: Every register row passes from its source VLAN, every probed unregistered path fails with a logged deny, and directory discovery works across the routed network.
lessons.evidence: Keep the test matrix with timestamps, the time queries, the deny-log captures, and the cross-VLAN SRV and CRL retrieval output.

model.label: the attack drill
model.text: Six attempts that your ACLs and host firewalls must stop. Use them as your denial tests.

quizzes.question: What is the complete evidence for one denial?
answers: The failed connection test paired with its entry in the router's deny log
A screenshot of the register
The absence of complaints
quizzes.explanation: The failed probe shows the client's view; the log shows the boundary made the decision. Together they prove enforcement.

quizzes.question: Why does the matrix test time with w32tm /stripchart rather than Test-NetConnection?
answers: Test-NetConnection is slower
NTP runs over UDP 123 and Test-NetConnection only probes TCP, so w32tm sends real time queries
w32tm also checks DNS
quizzes.explanation: Honest evidence names what a test can and cannot show — the same habit the identity course taught. A TCP probe to port 123 would prove nothing about a UDP service.

quizzes.question: A registered path fails during the matrix run. What is that?
answers: Expected behavior
A finding to resolve before the course ends
A reason to delete the register row quietly
quizzes.explanation: The register is the intended state. Reality disagreeing with it is exactly what the matrix exists to catch.

recap: Permits proven per VLAN; denials proven with their log entries.
Directory discovery and CRL retrieval work across the boundary.
Register and reality reconcile before the course moves on.
lessons.next: Lesson 6 locks down the router's own management — the one system that enforces everyone else's rules.

lessons.title: Protect the router's own management
lessons.summary: The router enforces every boundary, so whoever manages it controls them all. Give its management a separate network, a short list of who may reach it, a log of every change, and a versioned copy of every configuration.
objectives: Move the router's management interface onto a dedicated management VLAN.
Restrict management access to the Tier 0 administration seat and secure protocols.
Log router changes and keep versioned, hashed configuration backups.
steps: Create management VLAN 100 (10.0.100.0/24) for network-device management only, and bind the router's SSH and HTTPS management to its address there, 10.0.100.1. Disable Telnet, plain HTTP, and every management service the platform enables by default that the design does not use.

Permit management sessions to 10.0.100.1 only from AdminJumpBox01's planned address (10.0.60.10), which course 1.7 builds — until then, manage from the hypervisor console only. Add the row to the register: the router enforces Tier 0 boundaries, so its management is Tier 0.

Give each administrator a named account on the router and keep one sealed break-glass account; shared logins hide who changed what. Course 1.8 sends the router's syslog, including its deny log, to the collector; write that as a dated follow-up in the register now.

Export the running configuration after every approved change, hash it, and keep every version. Compare the newest export with the running configuration on a schedule; a difference with no change record is a finding.
lessons.command:
# From a host outside VLAN 100 (expected: TcpTestSucceeded False):
Test-NetConnection 10.0.100.1 -Port 22
# Configuration versions with hashes:
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\connect-segment\router-config-*.txt
lessons.check: Management answers only on VLAN 100 and only from the permitted source, insecure management services are off, and each configuration version has a hash and a matching change record.
lessons.evidence: Keep the management-access rule export, a refused connection test from a user VLAN, the list of disabled services, and the hashed configuration versions with their change records.

quizzes.question: Why does the router's management get its own VLAN?
answers: So user and server traffic can never reach the interface that changes the rules
Because routers cannot route their own traffic
To make the configuration file smaller
quizzes.explanation: A separate management network, reachable only from the admin plane, removes the most direct way to take over the device that enforces every boundary.

quizzes.question: Which tier manages the core router in this design?
answers: Tier 2, because every user depends on it
Tier 1, like any member server
Tier 0, because it enforces the boundaries that protect the domain controllers
quizzes.explanation: Anything that can change the protections around Tier 0 can control Tier 0. The router's access lists are one of those protections.

quizzes.question: The running configuration differs from the latest backup, and there is no change record. What is it?
answers: Normal drift
A finding to investigate
Proof that backups work
quizzes.explanation: Every change should be approved and recorded. An unexplained difference means either a missed record or an unauthorized change.

recap: Router management lives on VLAN 100, reachable from the Tier 0 seat only.
Insecure management services are off; logins are named, with one sealed break-glass account.
Every configuration version is hashed and tied to a change record.
lessons.next: The final lesson runs the change-triggered scans this network addition owes the 1.3 cadence.

lessons.title: Delta scan the change and hand off
lessons.summary: Course 1.3's rule was simple: every role addition gets a scan. Two systems joined the network and every existing one gained a gateway — that is a change worth measuring.
objectives: Run the change-triggered scans on the touched Windows systems.
Capture and hash the router configuration as its own baseline.
Hand the register and evidence into the standing cadence.
steps: Rescan both domain controllers with the same benchmark and tool versions as course 1.3, and take SBD-TIME01's first baseline scan. Attribute any movement to this course's changes — the gateway and time settings are the expected deltas.

Export the router's configuration, hash the export, and store it with the evidence. The router has no Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) benchmark in this lab, so its config export, register reconciliation, and deny log stand as its assessable record — say so explicitly in the evidence notes.

Add the new rows to the hardening course's exception and deviation record where the two overlap (time settings, any firewall interplay), and set the register's named owner and review date alongside the scan cadence.
Write the handoff line for the next course: the network now routes, filters, and keeps time — course 1.6's PKI publication host and template administration build on exactly these paths.
lessons.command:
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\connect-segment -Recurse | Select-Object Name, LastWriteTime
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\connect-segment\*
lessons.check: The DC rescans show only the expected deltas, TIME01 has a dated baseline, the router export is hashed and reconciled with the register, and owners and review dates are set.
lessons.evidence: Finish the course checklist: scan results, router export and hash, the reconciled register with owner and review date, and the handoff note.

quizzes.question: Why does this course end with scans at all?
answers: Scans are only for domain controllers
The 1.3 cadence is change-triggered, and this course changed every system's network posture
A vendor release required it this week
quizzes.explanation: The cadence from the hardening course is event-driven: a new gateway on every host and two new systems is exactly such an event.

quizzes.question: The router has no SCAP benchmark here. What stands in as its assessable record?
answers: Nothing — unscannable systems are exempt
Its hashed configuration export, the register reconciliation, and the deny log
A photo of the VM console
quizzes.explanation: Evidence is whatever lets a reviewer verify the state. For the router, that is its exported configuration tied to the register it enforces.

quizzes.question: Which earlier record absorbs this course's time and firewall decisions?
answers: The hardening course's exception and deviation record
The workbook from course 1.1 only
The offline root's ceremony log
quizzes.explanation: One living exception record, started in 1.3, keeps every deliberate departure in a single place the authorization path can assess.

recap: Change-triggered scans ran; deltas are attributed.
The router's record is its hashed export plus the register and deny log.
Owners, review dates, and the handoff to course 1.6 are written.
