prerequisites: Complete courses 1.4 and 1.5: a working two-tier PKI and the routed, default-deny network with pki.sbd.test reachable over HTTP per the register.
Build SBD-PKI-MGMT01 as a hardened Windows Server 2025 member server at 10.0.30.30 in the Servers OU (course 1.7 moves it, with the issuing CA, to a Tier 0 Servers OU).
Have the issuing CA's AIA and CDP URL plan from course 1.4 at hand — the filenames published here must match those embedded URLs exactly.
labNote: This course finishes the PKI chapter: the pki.sbd.test publication site goes live on SBD-PKI-MGMT01, and certificate template administration moves to that host, off the issuing CA. Publication stays plain HTTP by design — clients must be able to fetch revocation data before they can validate any certificate.

sources.title: Microsoft · What's new in Windows Server 2025

lessons.title: Build the pki.sbd.test publication site
lessons.summary: Every certificate the issuing CA has signed carries the pki.sbd.test URLs inside it. This lesson gives those URLs a real home: a small web site on SBD-PKI-MGMT01 serving certificates and revocation lists to the whole network.
objectives: Stand up the HTTP publication site on SBD-PKI-MGMT01.
Confirm the DNS alias from course 1.2 points at the publication host.
Explain why CDP and AIA publication uses HTTP, not HTTPS.
steps: On SBD-PKI-MGMT01, install the Web Server role and create a site (or virtual directory) whose folder will hold the published certificates and revocation lists. Serve .cer, .crt, and .crl files; nothing else belongs in this directory.
Confirm the pki.sbd.test alias from course 1.2 resolves to 10.0.30.30 from a client in another VLAN, and that the register's HTTP row from course 1.5 permits the path.

Leave the site on plain HTTP. Revocation checking has to work before any certificate can be trusted — putting the CRL behind HTTPS creates a loop where validating the site needs the very file it serves.
Restrict who can write to the publication folder: the CA's publishing process and the PKI administrators, nobody else. Clients read; they never write.
lessons.command:
Resolve-DnsName pki.sbd.test
Test-NetConnection pki.sbd.test -Port 80
Get-Website | Select-Object Name, State, PhysicalPath
lessons.check: pki.sbd.test resolves to the publication host from outside VLAN 30, the site answers on port 80, and the publication folder's permissions separate writers from readers.
lessons.evidence: Record the site configuration, folder permissions, the DNS resolution output from a cross-VLAN client, and the register row that permits the path.

quizzes.question: Why does the publication site stay on plain HTTP?
answers: HTTPS licenses cost money
Clients need the CRL to validate certificates — serving it over HTTPS creates a dependency loop
HTTP is faster than HTTPS in every case
quizzes.explanation: Revocation data must be reachable before trust can be evaluated. The files are public and signed; integrity comes from the signatures, not the transport.

quizzes.question: What belongs in the publication directory?
answers: Public CA certificates and CRLs only
The issuing CA's private key backup
Administrator scripts and passwords
quizzes.explanation: The same rule as course 1.4: clients need the public trust artifacts; secrets never enter a client-readable path.

quizzes.question: Which earlier work made this lesson a one-page job?
answers: Nothing — it stands alone
Course 1.1's domain controller promotion
The DNS alias reserved in 1.2 and the HTTP register row from 1.5
quizzes.explanation: pki.sbd.test was reserved two courses ago and the path through the boundary was registered in 1.5 — the sequence pays off here.

recap: pki.sbd.test now answers from SBD-PKI-MGMT01 over HTTP.
Only public artifacts live in the folder; only PKI processes write to it.
The transport is HTTP on purpose — revocation precedes trust.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 fills the site with the real trust data and proves the embedded URLs work.

lessons.title: Publish the trust data at its advertised URLs
lessons.summary: A publication site is only correct when the filenames it serves match the URLs the certificates already carry. Copy the current certificates and CRLs into place, wire the issuing CA to keep them fresh, and prove retrieval from a client that has never cached anything.
objectives: Publish the root and issuing certificates and current CRLs at the exact embedded URLs.
Configure the issuing CA to refresh its published files automatically.
Prove live retrieval and chain building from a cross-VLAN client.
steps: Compare the issuing CA's configured AIA and CDP URLs against the publication folder's layout. Every embedded URL must map to a real file path on the site — the filenames are not yours to improve.

Copy the current root certificate, root CRL, issuing certificate, and issuing CRL into the folder. The root's files still arrive by approved media; the issuing CA's can be written directly by its publishing process.
Configure the issuing CA's CRL publication to write into the site's folder on its schedule, so each new CRL replaces the old file at the same name before it expires.
From a clean client in another VLAN, fetch each URL and run the full verification: the chain must build and revocation data must come from the live site, not a cache.
lessons.command:
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\pki\test.cer
certutil -URL http://pki.sbd.test/RootCA.crl
Get-ChildItem C:\inetpub\pkiroot | Select-Object Name, LastWriteTime
lessons.check: Every AIA and CDP URL embedded in issued certificates returns the current file, urlfetch verification passes from a cross-VLAN client, and the CRL refresh lands at the same filename automatically.
lessons.evidence: Keep the URL-to-file mapping table, the folder listing with timestamps, and the urlfetch output from the clean client.

model.label: Use a web app, step 3
model.text: A client checks revocation at the URL you publish on pki.sbd.test.

quizzes.question: Why can't the published filenames be renamed to something tidier?
answers: The web server forbids renames
Issued certificates already embed the exact URLs; clients fetch those literally
The hardening baseline assigns the filenames
quizzes.explanation: The same lesson course 1.4 taught at signing time: extensions are fixed at issuance, so publication conforms to them, never the reverse.

quizzes.question: How do new root CRLs reach the site in this lab?
answers: By approved removable media from the offline ceremony
Over a direct network share from the root
They never need refreshing
quizzes.explanation: The root has no network path. Its refreshed CRL travels like everything else that crosses that boundary — reviewed, hashed, carried.

quizzes.question: What does certutil -verify -urlfetch add over opening the certificate?
answers: It prints the certificate in color
Nothing
It follows the embedded URLs live, proving publication and reachability rather than cached trust
quizzes.explanation: The -urlfetch option is the end-to-end test: chain building plus live AIA and CDP retrieval through the routed network.

recap: Published filenames mirror the embedded URLs exactly.
The issuing CA refreshes its files on schedule; the root's arrive by media.
A clean cross-VLAN client proves the chain and live revocation.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 moves template administration off the CA and onto this host.

lessons.title: Separate template administration
lessons.summary: Certificate templates are directory objects, and whoever edits them decides what the PKI will sign. Give that power its own seat — SBD-PKI-MGMT01 — with named administrators, instead of leaving it wherever a CA console happens to be open.
objectives: Establish SBD-PKI-MGMT01 as the only administration seat for templates.
Delegate template permissions to a named PKI administrators group.
Record the template change process before any template changes.
steps: Install the certificate management tools on SBD-PKI-MGMT01 and confirm the Certificate Templates console can read the directory's template store from there.

Create a PKI administrators group in the directory, place it under the Admin OU from course 1.3, and delegate the template permissions to that group — membership is the record of who may change what the CA signs.
Remove day-to-day template editing from everywhere else: the issuing CA's console stays for CA operations, not template design, and no Tier-0 account edits templates as routine work.

Write the change process: a template change names its requester, its reviewer, the versioning action (edit, duplicate, or supersede), and lands in the evidence record like any other configuration change.
lessons.command:
Get-ADGroup 'SBD PKI Admins' -Properties Members | Select-Object Name, Members
certutil -template | Select-String 'TemplatePropCommonName' | Select-Object -First 10
lessons.check: The templates console works from SBD-PKI-MGMT01, the PKI administrators group holds the delegated permissions, and the written change process names requester, reviewer, and versioning action.
lessons.evidence: Keep the delegation record, the group membership listing, and the signed-off template change process.

quizzes.question: Why do certificate templates deserve their own administration seat?
answers: Templates are directory objects that define what the CA will sign — editing them is a trust decision
The CA console cannot display templates
Templates take too much disk space on the CA
quizzes.explanation: A template edit changes what enrollment can produce. Separating the seat and naming the editors makes that power visible and auditable.

quizzes.question: Where does the PKI administrators group live?
answers: The default Users container
Under the Admin OU from course 1.3, with the other privileged groups
On the offline root
quizzes.explanation: The OU design already has a home for privileged identity — this group joins it so delegation and policy follow the same structure.

quizzes.question: A template needs a change. What is the first artifact?
answers: The edited template itself
A restart of Certificate Services
The change record: requester, reviewer, and the versioning action
quizzes.explanation: The record precedes the change, the same discipline as the course 1.5 exception register — configuration follows documentation, not the other way around.

recap: SBD-PKI-MGMT01 is the template administration seat.
A named group under the Admin OU holds the delegated power.
Template changes have a written process before they have edits.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 uses that process to publish the lab's first working templates.

lessons.title: Publish the first working templates
lessons.summary: The default template set is a menu, not a deployment. Duplicate the two templates this network actually needs — computer authentication and server authentication — set their cryptography deliberately, and publish only those.
objectives: Duplicate and configure the computer and web server templates against the approved plan.
Set key sizes and validity that satisfy the Windows Server 2025 minimums.
Publish only the needed templates, scoped to a pilot group first.
steps: From the administration seat, duplicate the Computer template as SBD Computer Authentication. Set the approved key provider, a key size of at least 2,048 bits, a validity period within course 1.4's one-to-two-year example, subject built from directory information, and autoenrollment permission for a pilot computer group only.

Duplicate the Web Server template as SBD Server Authentication for the business services in course 1.11: enrollment permission for the server administrators, no autoenrollment, and exportable keys only if the recovery plan explicitly says so.
Record each template's version, settings, and justification through the lesson-3 change process before publishing.
Publish exactly these two templates on the issuing CA and remove any default template the plan does not call for — an unpublished template cannot be mis-enrolled.
lessons.command:
certutil -CATemplates -config 'SBD-SUBCA01\SBD Issuing CA'
certutil -template 'SBDComputerAuthentication' | Select-String 'msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag','msPKI-Minimal-Key-Size'
lessons.check: The CA publishes exactly the two planned templates, each shows the approved key size and permissions, and both carry a completed change record.
lessons.evidence: Keep each template's configuration export, its change record, and the CA's published-template listing.

quizzes.question: Why duplicate the built-in templates instead of editing them?
answers: Built-ins cannot be published at all
Duplication preserves the originals and gives your version its own name, version, and record
Duplicates issue faster
quizzes.explanation: Working on a named copy keeps the baseline intact and makes your settings — and their history — unmistakably yours.

quizzes.question: What floor applies to the template key sizes on this network?
answers: 512 bits for speed
1,024 bits
2,048-bit RSA at minimum — Windows Server 2025 enforces it for TLS server authentication
quizzes.explanation: Windows Server 2025 requires at least 2,048-bit RSA keys for TLS server authentication, so a plan below that produces certificates the platform itself will reject.

quizzes.question: Why publish to a pilot group before the whole domain?
answers: A small blast radius proves the template before autoenrollment touches fifty machines in course 1.9
Pilots are a licensing requirement
Templates expire if unused
quizzes.explanation: The fleet course will turn autoenrollment loose at scale. Proving the template on a pilot first is the same test-then-widen habit as the Group Policy work.

recap: Two named templates exist, configured on purpose, nothing else published.
Key sizes meet the 2025 floor; permissions are pilot-scoped.
Every template carries its change record.
lessons.next: The final lesson proves enrollment end to end and runs the delta scans.

lessons.title: Validate enrollment and delta scan
lessons.summary: Close the loop the way course 1.4 did, but now across the routed network: a pilot machine enrolls automatically, validates against the live publication site, and the change-triggered scans record what this course did.
objectives: Prove pilot autoenrollment through the published template.
Verify chain and revocation against pki.sbd.test from the enrolled client.
Run the course's delta scans and file the evidence.
steps: Enable the autoenrollment policy for the pilot computer group, refresh policy on a pilot machine, and confirm it receives an SBD Computer Authentication certificate without a human touching the request.
On that machine, run the full verification: the chain must reach the approved root and every revocation URL must answer from pki.sbd.test across the boundary.
Rescan SBD-SUBCA01 and take SBD-PKI-MGMT01's first baseline with the same benchmark and tool versions as always; the publication site and template changes are the expected deltas.
File the course evidence: enrollment output, urlfetch results, template records, and the scan set — the PKI chapter is finished.
lessons.command:
gpupdate /force
certutil -pulse
Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My | Select-Object Subject, NotAfter, Thumbprint
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\pki\pilot.cer
lessons.check: The pilot enrolls hands-free, verification passes with live retrieval from pki.sbd.test, and both VLAN 30 hosts have current, attributed scan results.
lessons.evidence: Keep the pilot's certificate details, the urlfetch output, and the delta-scan comparison for SUBCA01 plus the PKI-MGMT01 baseline.

model.label: What if a certificate expired?
model.text: The network permits the connection; the client refuses the expired certificate.

quizzes.question: What does a hands-free pilot enrollment prove?
answers: Template permissions, autoenrollment policy, the CA, DNS, and the routed path all agree — the whole chain works
Only that Group Policy refreshed
That the root CA is online
quizzes.explanation: Autoenrollment succeeds only when every layer this path has built cooperates — which is exactly why it is the closing test.

quizzes.question: Which hosts get scanned at the end of this course?
answers: Only the pilot workstation
SBD-SUBCA01 (rescan) and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 (first baseline)
The offline root over the network
quizzes.explanation: The cadence is change-triggered: the CA changed and a new host joined, so one rescan and one baseline.

quizzes.question: What makes the PKI chapter complete at the end of this course?
answers: The 3D model updates itself
Fifty workstations are joined
Publication, template administration, and working enrollment — the PKI chapter's remaining pieces — are all in evidence
quizzes.explanation: Course 1.4 built the hierarchy; this course finished its services. The courses that follow can rely on certificates as a solved problem.

recap: Pilot autoenrollment works end to end across the routed network.
Live revocation retrieval from pki.sbd.test is proven, not assumed.
Delta scans and evidence close the PKI chapter.

Decide the privileged accounts: separate admin identities per tier, never daily-driver accounts with admin rights.
labNote: This course builds the control plane before the fleet exists: DHCP for the workstation VLAN, and a tiered administration model where privileged sessions only ever start from dedicated hosts. lessons.title: Design the tiers and the address plan
lessons.summary: Tiering is one sentence with teeth: credentials that control a tier never touch a less-trusted one. Write that policy against the OU structure, then plan the DHCP scope the fleet will live in — both before any host is built.
objectives: Define the tiers and map each to systems, OUs, and admin accounts.
Write the credential rule each tier enforces.
Plan the VLAN 80 DHCP scope, options, and relay.
steps: Define three tiers against what exists, using Microsoft's rule: anything that can control a Tier 0 system is Tier 0. Tier 0 is the identity and trust fabric (DCs, both CAs, PKI-MGMT01) plus what controls it — the hypervisor hosts and their console, the core router's management, and the DC-facing parts of the tools that patch, protect, scan, monitor, and back up the DCs. Tier 1 is the member servers; Tier 2 the user endpoints. Map each tier to its OUs: Tier 0 to the Domain Controllers OU plus a new Tier 0 Servers OU for SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 (lesson 4 moves them out of the Servers OU), Tier 1 to the Servers OU, and Tier 2 to the Workstations OU.

Write the credential rule per tier: a Tier 0 account signs in only on Tier 0 systems and AdminJumpBox01; Tier 1 admins work from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01; Tier 2 from SBD-ADMIN-PC01. The audit custodian uses separate accounts and sessions on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 that ordinary server operators cannot use. Each administrator gets separate per-tier accounts — the daily account holds no admin rights anywhere.

Plan the DHCP design: scope 10.0.80.100–199 for the workstation VLAN — 100 addresses, room for the 50 PCs, the test clients, and replacement machines whose old leases have not yet expired — with options for router 10.0.80.1, the two DCs as DNS, and the sbd.test domain; the core router relays VLAN 80 broadcasts to SBD-DHCP01; everything else stays static.

Add the register rows this course needs: VLAN 60 to each tier's management ports (rules A01–A04 in Inside the Network), DHCP relay from the core to SBD-DHCP01 (F04), and explicit denies from VLAN 80 into VLAN 60 — user space never initiates toward the admin plane.
lessons.command:
# Capture the design inputs: OU targets and current account separation.
Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter * | Select-Object Name, DistinguishedName
Get-ADGroupMember 'Domain Admins' | Select-Object Name, SamAccountName
lessons.check: The tier map names systems, OUs, admin hosts, and accounts for every tier; the DHCP plan is written; and the register has the new permit and deny rows with owners.
lessons.evidence: Keep the tier access matrix, the per-administrator account plan, the DHCP scope design, and the updated register rows.

quizzes.question: What is the one-sentence tiering rule?
answers: Admins should use strong passwords
Credentials that control a tier never sign in to a less-trusted tier
Every admin needs Domain Admin rights
quizzes.explanation: Everything else in the model — hosts, OUs, logon policies — exists to enforce that single sentence.

quizzes.question: Why does each administrator get separate per-tier accounts?
answers: So a credential captured on a lower tier cannot open a higher one
Licensing counts accounts per tier
Password policies require it
quizzes.explanation: Credential theft travels with sign-ins. Separate accounts bound what any one capture is worth.

quizzes.question: Which direction does the register explicitly deny?
answers: Admin VLAN to the tiers it manages
DCs to anything
User VLAN 80 initiating into the admin VLAN 60
quizzes.explanation: The admin plane reaches down to manage; user space never reaches up. The deny row makes that a logged fact, not an intention.

quizzes.question: SBD-WSUS01 approves the updates the domain controllers install. Which tier administers the domain controllers' update ring?
answers: Tier 1, because WSUS is a member server
Tier 0, because anything that can push code to a DC can control it
Tier 2, because updates start on workstations
quizzes.explanation: Microsoft's tier model treats systems that patch, scan, monitor, protect, back up, or host Tier 0 as Tier 0. The DC-facing scope of a tool belongs to Tier 0 even when the server itself sits in a member-server VLAN.

recap: Three tiers, each with its systems, OU, admin host, and accounts.
The credential rule is written before any host enforces it.
DHCP scope, options, relay, and register rows are planned.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 builds the DHCP service the fleet will depend on.

lessons.title: Build SBD-DHCP01 and the relay
lessons.summary: Addressing is the first service fifty machines will ask for. Build the DHCP server, authorize it in the directory so rogue servers stand out, and relay VLAN 80's broadcasts through the core.
objectives: Install and authorize the DHCP role on SBD-DHCP01.
Create the VLAN 80 scope with the planned options.
Configure the core relay and prove a lease end to end.
steps: Install the DHCP role on SBD-DHCP01 in the Servers OU and complete directory authorization — an unauthorized Windows DHCP server refuses to serve domain networks, the directory's built-in check against rogue DHCP servers.
Create the IPv4 scope 10.0.80.100–199 with the planned options: router 10.0.80.1, DNS 10.0.10.10 and 10.0.10.11, domain sbd.test. Leave every other VLAN static as designed.
Configure dynamic DNS updates using a dedicated low-privilege credential so client records register securely in the sbd.test zone from course 1.2.

Enable the DHCP relay on the core router's VLAN 80 interface toward 10.0.20.10, confirm the register row (F04) permits it, then pull a lease with a temporary test VM in VLAN 80 and watch its A record appear.
lessons.command:
Get-DhcpServerInDC
Get-DhcpServerv4Scope | Select-Object ScopeId, StartRange, EndRange, State
Get-DhcpServerv4OptionValue -ScopeId 10.0.80.0 | Select-Object OptionId, Value
Resolve-DnsName sbd-test80.sbd.test
lessons.check: The server shows as authorized, the scope serves the planned range and options through the relay, and the test client's secure dynamic DNS record exists on both DCs.
lessons.evidence: Record the authorization output, scope and option configuration, the relay setting on the core, and the test lease with its DNS registration.

quizzes.question: What does directory authorization of a DHCP server give you?
answers: Faster leases
A built-in check that makes unauthorized Windows DHCP servers refuse to serve the domain
Larger scopes
quizzes.explanation: Authorization is the directory's rogue-DHCP control — a one-click setting with a real security story behind it.

quizzes.question: Why does the relay exist at all?
answers: DHCP broadcasts do not cross the router, so the core forwards VLAN 80's requests to the server in VLAN 20
It encrypts DHCP traffic
Relays make addresses permanent
quizzes.explanation: Broadcasts stop at the VLAN boundary. The relay is the deliberate, registered exception that carries them to SBD-DHCP01.

quizzes.question: Why use a dedicated credential for dynamic DNS updates?
answers: The server cannot update DNS otherwise
It speeds up record creation
Record ownership and updates trace to one low-privilege identity instead of a powerful computer account
quizzes.explanation: Secure updates from course 1.2 are only as accountable as the identity writing them — a scoped credential keeps that clean.

recap: SBD-DHCP01 is authorized, scoped, and serving through the relay.
Options hand out the gateway, both DCs, and the domain.
A test lease proved addressing and secure DNS registration together.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 builds the three systems the administrators will work from.

lessons.title: Build the administration systems
lessons.summary: Privileged work gets dedicated, hardened seats: one jump host for Tier 0, one workstation for server administration, one for endpoint administration — each in the Admin OU, each doing nothing else.
objectives: Link the hardening policies to the Admin OU's computer sub-OUs, then build the three VLAN 60 systems into them.
Keep them single-purpose: hardened, minimal, no user-space services.
Register and restrict their management paths.
steps: Create two computer sub-OUs under the Admin OU — Admin Servers for AdminJumpBox01 and SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, Admin Workstations for SBD-ADMIN-PC01 — and link course 1.3's Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) Group Policy objects (GPOs) to them before any seat joins: the member-server policies to Admin Servers and the Windows 11 policies from the same package to Admin Workstations. Course 1.3 linked them only to the Domain Controllers and Servers OUs, so without this step the seats would boot unhardened.

Build AdminJumpBox01, SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and SBD-ADMIN-PC01 as clean Windows Server 2025 (or Windows 11, for the endpoint seat) installs and join each into its sub-OU, so the hardening applies from first boot.

Strip them to purpose: no browsing to anything but internal admin interfaces, no mail, no file shares hosted, and the management tools for exactly their tier — Remote Server Administration Tools (RSAT) on the server seats, endpoint tooling on the PC seat.

Register the management paths: VLAN 60 to Tier 0 and Tier 1 ports (remote desktop 3389, remote management 5985–5986, SSH 22 for the domain-joined Linux servers) from the specific admin host each tier allows, and the router's management on VLAN 100 from AdminJumpBox01 only. Keep the VLAN 80 → VLAN 60 deny from lesson 1 in force.
Require the admin hosts' own local firewalls to accept management inbound from nowhere — sessions originate here, they never terminate here.
lessons.command:
Get-ADComputer -SearchBase 'OU=Admin,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter * | Select-Object Name, DistinguishedName
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Admin Servers,OU=Admin,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Admin Workstations,OU=Admin,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
Test-NetConnection SBD-DC01.sbd.test -Port 5985
gpresult /r /scope:computer
lessons.check: All three hosts sit in their Admin sub-OUs with the STIG GPOs linked there and applied, management ports answer from the correct admin host per tier, and nothing in user space can open a session toward VLAN 60.
lessons.evidence: Record each host's build sheet, OU placement, the sub-OU GPO links, gpresult output, and the register rows for its permitted management paths.

quizzes.question: Why do the admin hosts run nothing but administration?
answers: Extra software costs licenses
Every extra capability — mail, browsing, documents — is a way to phish or poison the most valuable sessions on the network
Admin tools conflict with browsers
quizzes.explanation: These hosts carry privileged credentials. Minimizing what runs on them minimizes what can steal from them.

quizzes.question: Which way do management sessions flow?
answers: From the admin hosts outward to their tier — never inbound to the admin hosts
In both directions equally
From workstations to the jump box
quizzes.explanation: The admin plane originates; it never serves. Inbound-nothing is what keeps a compromised endpoint from riding into VLAN 60.

quizzes.question: Why link the STIG GPOs to the Admin sub-OUs before the seats join?
answers: The seats cannot join the domain otherwise
The OU name requires it
Course 1.3 linked them only to the Domain Controllers and Servers OUs, so the seats would otherwise boot unhardened
quizzes.explanation: Policy follows links, not names. Linking first means each seat is STIG-configured from its first boot, before it ever does privileged work.

recap: Three single-purpose admin seats, hardened from first boot.
Management flows outward only; VLAN 60 accepts nothing inbound.
Every management path is a register row.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 makes the credential rule something the directory enforces.

lessons.title: Restrict where privilege can sign in
lessons.summary: The tier rule becomes real when the directory refuses the wrong sign-in. Give Tier 0 servers their own OU first, deny privileged logons on lower tiers by policy, protect the highest accounts, and make the refusal something you can show in a log.
objectives: Move the Tier 0 member servers into their own OU before any deny policy lands.
Enforce per-tier sign-in restrictions with Group Policy logon rights, and record the one network-logon exception.
Protect Tier 0 accounts and prove a cross-tier sign-in is denied and logged.
steps: Create the Tier 0 Servers OU (OU=Tier 0 Servers,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test) with deletion protection, link course 1.3's member-server STIG GPOs to it so nothing loses its hardening, and move SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 there. Both are Tier 0, and the Servers OU is about to deny Tier 0 sign-ins — left there, they would lock Tier 0 out of its own systems.

Create one tier logon GPO for the Servers OU — now Tier 1 only — and one for the Workstations OU, and never link either to the Domain Controllers or Tier 0 Servers OUs. User rights don't merge across GPOs: for each right, the highest-precedence GPO that sets it wins, so each list repeats the entries course 1.3's STIG GPO sets for that right (such as Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins), and the tier GPO links above the STIG GPO. On the Servers OU, give the Tier 0 admin group (SBD Tier 0 Admins in this sample) Deny log on locally, Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services, Deny log on as a batch job, and Deny log on as a service. On the Workstations OU, give both the Tier 0 and Tier 1 groups those four denies plus Deny access to this computer from the network.

On the Servers OU, set Deny access to this computer from the network — the Tier 0 group plus the STIG's entries — in a separate GPO that excludes the SBD Tier 0 Console Hosts group through security filtering (deny Apply group policy). Course 1.10 adds SBD-WSUS01 and SBD-EPO01 to that group, so those two keep only the STIG's own setting. From AdminJumpBox01, Tier 0 manages the domain controllers' WSUS update ring and their agent policy in Trellix ePolicy Orchestrator (ePO) through those two consoles, using Tier 0 task accounts outside Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins (which the STIG denies network logon on member servers); a Kerberos network logon leaves no reusable credentials on the server. Record the exception — the two servers, the accounts, the reason, and its owner — in the course 1.3 exception record.

Add Tier 0 administrators to the Protected Users group so the domain refuses their weaker authentication paths, and note the Windows Server 2025 behavior that supports this design: RC4 ticket-granting tickets are gone and legacy remote password changes are blocked for protected accounts. Protected Users accounts also cannot be delegated, which keeps the console exception free of reusable credentials.
Keep the built-in safety valves: one documented break-glass account, excluded from the deny policies, with its password sealed and its every use alarmed in a later logging course.

Record the multifactor decision the model calls for on VLAN 60 — smart card or certificate-based sign-in for privileged accounts is the natural follow-on to course 1.6's templates; write the decision and its target date even if implementation waits.
lessons.command:
Get-ADComputer -SearchBase 'OU=Tier 0 Servers,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter * | Select-Object Name
Get-ADGroupMember 'Protected Users' | Select-Object Name
# On the Tier 2 test machine: export the effective logon rights and read the deny lines.
secedit /export /mergedpolicy /cfg C:\Evidence\tiered-admin\user-rights.inf /areas user_rights
Select-String -Path C:\Evidence\tiered-admin\user-rights.inf -Pattern 'SeDeny'
(Get-ADGroup 'SBD Tier 0 Admins').SID.Value   # from an admin seat: this SID must appear on those lines
# After the refused Tier 0 sign-in: event 4625 with status 0xC000015B (logon type not granted).
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Where-Object Message -match '0xC000015B' | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id
lessons.check: SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 sit in the Tier 0 Servers OU and still accept Tier 0 sign-ins; on a Tier 2 test machine the deny rights list the Tier 0 group's SID, and a Tier 0 sign-in there is refused with Security event 4625 (status 0xC000015B); the console network-logon exception is in the exception record; Protected Users contains the Tier 0 admins; and the break-glass and MFA decisions are written.
lessons.evidence: Keep the Tier 0 Servers OU move, the logon-rights GPO reports with their links and security filtering, the user-rights export, the refused sign-in's 4625 event, the exception record entry, the Protected Users membership, and the break-glass and MFA decision records.

model.label: Attack drill, step 6
model.text: A stolen administrator session aims at a domain controller and is stopped. This is the path your logon restrictions close.

quizzes.question: What turns the tier rule from policy into enforcement?
answers: An email to administrators
Deny-logon rights applied by GPO at each lower tier's OU
Renaming the admin accounts
quizzes.explanation: The OU-linked deny rights are the mechanism: the directory itself refuses the out-of-tier sign-in.

quizzes.question: What does Protected Users membership buy a Tier 0 account?
answers: Faster sign-ins
Exemption from password changes
The domain refuses its weaker authentication paths, shrinking what a credential thief can replay
quizzes.explanation: Protected Users trades convenience for resistance — appropriate exactly for the accounts whose theft ends the network.

quizzes.question: Why does a break-glass account exist outside the deny policies?
answers: So a policy mistake cannot lock every administrator out — and its sealed, alarmed use keeps the exception honest
Because every admin wants one
Deny policies cannot apply to more than ten accounts
quizzes.explanation: Strict tiering needs one documented escape hatch. Sealing and alarming it is what keeps the hatch from becoming a habit.

quizzes.question: Why do SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 move out of the Servers OU before the deny policy is linked?
answers: The Servers OU has reached its size limit
They are Tier 0: the Servers OU now denies Tier 0 sign-ins, so they would lock Tier 0 out of its own systems
Certificate Services cannot run in an OU with linked policies
quizzes.explanation: Tier follows control, not hostname. Systems that control Tier 0 need an OU where Tier 0 can sign in and the lower-tier denies never apply.

quizzes.question: Why may Tier 0 still use a network logon on SBD-WSUS01 and SBD-EPO01?
answers: Tier 0 manages the DC update ring and DC agent policy there, and a Kerberos network logon leaves no reusable credentials on the server
Network logons are never logged
Those two servers are Tier 0 systems
quizzes.explanation: Interactive, Remote Desktop, batch, and service logons leave reusable credentials behind; a Kerberos network logon does not, and Protected Users accounts cannot be delegated. The exception is narrow, named, and recorded.

recap: Tier 0 servers have their own OU, so the deny policies never lock Tier 0 out.
Lower tiers refuse higher-tier credentials by policy, with events to prove it; the console network-logon exception is recorded.
Tier 0 accounts sit in Protected Users, backed by 2025's stricter defaults.
Break-glass and MFA are written decisions, not loose ends.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 tests the whole plane — the paths that must work and the sign-ins that must fail.

lessons.title: Prove the tiers and the addressing
lessons.summary: Run the matrix: every tier's administration works from its seat, every cross-tier attempt fails with an event, and the addressing service behaves exactly as registered.
objectives: Verify each tier's management path from its designated seat.
Capture the denial evidence for out-of-tier attempts.
Re-prove DHCP, relay, and dynamic DNS under the finished rules.
steps: From AdminJumpBox01, manage a DC and SBD-SUBCA01 with a Tier 0 account — the Tier 0 Servers OU kept that access; from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, manage SBD-DHCP01 with a Tier 1 account; from SBD-ADMIN-PC01, manage the VLAN 80 test client with a Tier 2 account. Record each success with its session details, including the target's Security event 4624 (and 4672, which marks a logon that received special privileges).

Attempt the forbidden combinations — Tier 0 credentials at the test client, a session from VLAN 80 toward VLAN 60 — and capture both the refusal the user sees and the record the infrastructure writes: Security event 4625 with status 0xC000015B on the test client for the refused sign-in, and the router's deny-log entry for the VLAN 80 session.
Renew the test client's lease and confirm options, registration, and the relay still behave with all restrictions active; the control plane must not have broken the service plane.
Reconcile the tier access matrix against what you just proved and file it with the register — the two documents together are the admin plane's assessable record.
lessons.command:
Enter-PSSession SBD-DHCP01.sbd.test   # from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, Tier 1 account
ipconfig /renew   # on the VLAN 80 test client
# On the test client: refused sign-ins in the last hour (status 0xC000015B = logon type not granted).
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Where-Object Message -match '0xC000015B' | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id
lessons.check: Every in-tier path succeeds, every tested out-of-tier path fails with captured evidence, and DHCP with dynamic DNS still works end to end under the full rule set.
lessons.evidence: Keep the completed tier matrix with timestamps, the denial captures, and the post-restriction lease and registration proof.

model.label: What if a PC tries remote desktop to another PC?
model.text: Host firewalls stop lateral movement between workstations.

quizzes.question: What pairs make the denial evidence complete?
answers: Two screenshots of the same error
The user-visible refusal plus the infrastructure's event or deny-log entry
A verbal report
quizzes.explanation: Same standard as course 1.5: the client's view shows the attempt, the log shows the boundary deciding — together they prove enforcement.

quizzes.question: Why re-test DHCP after the restrictions landed?
answers: Hardening the control plane can accidentally break the service plane — proving both still work is the point
Leases expire during lessons
The relay resets daily
quizzes.explanation: Every tightening risks collateral damage. The matrix ends with services proven healthy, not presumed.

quizzes.question: What is the admin plane's assessable record?
answers: The jump box's wallpaper
A list of administrator names
The tier access matrix reconciled with the ACL register
quizzes.explanation: Who may manage what, from where, over which path — matrix plus register answers it in a form an assessor can test.

recap: In-tier works, out-of-tier fails, and both are on record.
Addressing and registration survived the restrictions.
Matrix and register reconcile as one assessable story.
lessons.next: The final lesson runs the scans and hands a managed, addressable network to course 1.8.

lessons.title: Delta scan and hand off
lessons.summary: Four new systems joined and the directory's logon policy changed — the cadence fires again. Baseline the newcomers, rescan what changed, and hand the next course a network that can finally be watched from somewhere safe.
objectives: Baseline the four new hosts and rescan the changed ones.
Fold the course's decisions into the standing records.
Write the handoff course 1.8 builds on.
steps: Run first baselines on SBD-DHCP01 and the three admin hosts with the standard benchmark and tool versions, and rescan SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 — the move to the Tier 0 Servers OU is their change, and the rescan should show their hardening intact.

Add this course's rows to the living records: the deny-logon and Protected Users decisions into the exception record where they interact with STIG values, beside lesson 4's console network-logon exception, and the new permit and deny rows into the register with owners.
Confirm the admin hosts appear in the hardening course's quarterly cadence; privileged seats are rescanned first from now on, not last.

Write the handoff: administration now has a home, which means the logging course can require that SIEM consoles and collectors are managed only from VLAN 60 — with the DC-facing scopes from the Tier 0 seat and audit retention under the custodian's separate accounts — say so explicitly for course 1.8.
lessons.command:
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\tiered-admin -Recurse | Select-Object Name, LastWriteTime
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\tiered-admin\*
lessons.check: Four baselines and the Tier 0 server rescans are filed with attributed deltas, the exception record and register carry the new rows, and the handoff names the logging course's management constraint.
lessons.evidence: Finish the checklist: scan set, updated records, the tier matrix, and the handoff note.

quizzes.question: Which systems are rescanned, not baselined, this time?
answers: SBD-SUBCA01 and SBD-PKI-MGMT01 — they moved to the Tier 0 Servers OU
The brand-new admin hosts
The offline root
quizzes.explanation: New host, new baseline; changed host, rescan. The two Tier 0 servers changed OU, so the rescan proves the move kept their hardening.

quizzes.question: Why do the privileged seats move to the front of the quarterly cadence?
answers: They have the fastest disks
They carry the credentials that control everything else — drift there costs the most
Scanners work alphabetically
quizzes.explanation: Scan priority follows consequence. The hosts that hold Tier 0 sessions earn the first look every quarter.

quizzes.question: What does this course hand to course 1.8?
answers: Fifty workstations
The business services
A safe management plane — collectors and SIEM consoles can now be administered only from VLAN 60
quizzes.explanation: Logging infrastructure is a target; building it after the admin plane means it is managed safely from day one.

recap: Baselines, rescans, and attributed deltas are on file.
Exception record and register absorbed the course's decisions.
Course 1.8 inherits a managed, addressable network.
lessons.next: That completes course 1.7. Course 1.8 builds the logging pipeline — collect, protect, analyze — before the fleet arrives to be watched.

prerequisites: Complete course 1.7: the admin plane exists, and this course's systems are managed only from VLAN 60.

Provision SBD-SYSLOG01 (10.0.20.20) as Windows Server 2025, SBD-SPLUNK01 (10.0.50.10) on Linux joined to the sbd.test domain with its time service (chrony or ntpd) pointed at both domain controllers, and SBD-AUDIT01 (10.0.50.40) as Windows Server 2025 joined to the domain.
Have the course 1.5 register ready for the new rows: event forwarding to the collector, syslog from the core router, and the forwarder path into the analysis system.
labNote: This course builds the model's collect → protect → analyze chain before the fleet arrives, so every later system is observed from its first boot. Collection is configuration you can show; protection is permissions and retention you can defend; analysis is a search someone actually runs.

lessons.title: Design collect, protect, analyze
lessons.summary: Three systems, three distinct jobs: SBD-SYSLOG01 gathers, SBD-AUDIT01 preserves, SBD-SPLUNK01 answers questions. Decide what is collected first, how long it lives, and who may touch which stage — before a single event flows.
objectives: Assign the three roles and the first collection scope.
Decide retention, protection, and access per stage.
Register the pipeline's network paths.
steps: Write the role sentence for each host: the collector receives Windows events and the core router's syslog; the repository holds the protected, long-retention copy; the analysis system indexes a working copy for search and alerting. One copy to keep, one copy to question.

Scope the first collection to what already produces evidence: both DCs' Security logs, the core router's deny log from course 1.5, and the admin hosts' sign-in events — the fleet joins this scope in the next course, not now.

Decide the AU-family answers and write them down: retention length per stage, who may read each stage, and that nobody — including administrators — writes or deletes in the repository outside the archival process (that is the AU-9 protection story).

Add the register rows: DC and admin-host event forwarding to the collector (WinRM 5985), router syslog UDP 514 to the collector, and the forwarder path from collector to the analysis system; all three systems are managed only from VLAN 60 per course 1.7's handoff.
lessons.command:
# Capture the before state: what the DCs currently audit and where nothing is forwarded yet.
auditpol /get /category:* | Select-String 'Logon|Account Management|Directory Service|Policy Change'
Get-Service Wecsvc -ComputerName SBD-SYSLOG01
lessons.check: The design names each stage's job, scope, retention, and readers; the repository's no-delete rule is written; and the register carries the three pipeline paths with owners.
lessons.evidence: Keep the pipeline design sheet, the retention and access table, and the new register rows.

model.label: Turn an event into evidence
model.text: Follow one event from a domain controller to the collector, Splunk, and the audit copy.

quizzes.question: Why separate the repository from the analysis system?
answers: The protected record and the working copy have different jobs — tampering with searches must never mean tampering with evidence
Splunk cannot store data
Two systems are cheaper than one
quizzes.explanation: Analysis needs flexibility; the record needs integrity. Splitting them means a compromised search tier still leaves the evidence intact.

quizzes.question: What is in the first collection scope?
answers: Every system including the unbuilt fleet
The sources that already produce evidence: DC Security logs, the router's deny log, and admin-host sign-ins
Only the collector's own log
quizzes.explanation: Collect what exists and matters most. The fleet widens the scope in course 1.9 — into a pipeline already proven.

quizzes.question: Who may delete from SBD-AUDIT01?
answers: Any Domain Admin
The analysis system automatically
Nobody outside the written archival process — that restriction is the protection control
quizzes.explanation: AU-9 in one sentence: the record survives its administrators. Deletion happens only by the documented retention process.

recap: Collector gathers, repository preserves, analysis answers.
Scope starts with the DCs, the router denies, and the admin plane.
Retention, readers, and the no-delete rule are written; paths are registered.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 makes sure the right events exist before anything forwards them.

lessons.title: Turn on the right auditing
lessons.summary: Forwarding garbage faster is not monitoring. Set the advanced audit policy so the events that tell the network's story — sign-ins, account changes, directory changes, policy changes — actually get written.
objectives: Apply the advanced audit policy categories the design needs.
Reconcile audit settings with the course 1.3 Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) values.
Verify effective auditing on the DCs and admin hosts.
steps: Review what the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Group Policy objects (GPOs) from course 1.3 already audit — much of the advanced audit policy arrived with the STIGs. This lesson reconciles and fills gaps rather than starting over.

Confirm the categories the design depends on are at least at the STIG values on the DCs: Logon/Logoff, Account Management, Directory Service Changes, and Policy Change — success and failure where the design says so.
Extend the same policy to the admin hosts' OU so privileged sessions write the sign-in trail lesson 5 of course 1.7 started capturing by hand.
Any place this course wants more auditing than the STIG sets, make it a documented addition in the GPO structure — never a local, invisible tweak — and note it in the exception/addition record.
lessons.command:
auditpol /get /subcategory:'Logon','User Account Management','Directory Service Changes','Audit Policy Change'
gpresult /r /scope:computer
lessons.check: Effective audit policy on the DCs and admin hosts covers the designed categories at or above the STIG values, applied through GPO, with any additions documented.
lessons.evidence: Keep the auditpol output per host class, the GPO report, and the documented additions.

quizzes.question: Why start from the course 1.3 GPOs instead of a fresh audit policy?
answers: Fresh policies are forbidden
The STIGs already set most of it — reconciling avoids conflicts and double-maintenance
auditpol cannot show existing settings
quizzes.explanation: The hardening baseline was the first word on auditing. This lesson's job is alignment and gaps, not a rival policy.

quizzes.question: Where do audit-policy additions get made?
answers: In the GPO structure, documented — never as local tweaks
Directly in each server's local policy
In the collector's configuration
quizzes.explanation: Local tweaks drift and hide. Policy through GPO keeps the audit posture visible, scanned, and reproducible.

quizzes.question: Which event families does the design treat as the core story?
answers: Print spooler events
Disk defragmentation logs
Sign-ins, account management, directory changes, and policy changes
quizzes.explanation: Who authenticated, who changed an account, who touched the directory, who altered policy — that is the identity network's narrative.

recap: Audit policy is reconciled with the STIG baseline, not reinvented.
DCs and admin hosts write the designed event families.
Additions are GPO-visible and documented.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 builds the collector those events will flow to.

lessons.title: Build the collector
lessons.summary: SBD-SYSLOG01 becomes the funnel: Windows Event Forwarding brings the DC and admin-host events in by subscription, and the core router's denies arrive as syslog — one host where the network's record first lands.
objectives: Configure the Windows Event Collector service and subscription.
Point the source hosts at the collector by GPO.
Receive the router's syslog deny stream.
steps: On SBD-SYSLOG01, enable the Windows Event Collector service and create a source-initiated subscription for the designed event IDs from the DCs and admin hosts, delivered into the Forwarded Events log.
By GPO on the relevant OUs, set the subscription manager to the collector and grant the Network Service read access to the Security log — the sources push; the collector never reaches into them.
Add a syslog intake on the collector for UDP 514 and point the core router's deny logging at it, so course 1.5's boundary decisions land beside the Windows record.
Confirm the register rows are the only paths in use: WinRM from the source OUs to the collector, syslog from the core, and nothing listening that the design didn't ask for.
lessons.command:
wecutil es
wecutil gs SBD-ForwardedSecurity
Get-WinEvent -LogName ForwardedEvents -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, MachineName
lessons.check: The subscription is active, events from both DCs and the admin hosts appear in Forwarded Events with correct source machine names, and router deny entries arrive on the syslog intake.
lessons.evidence: Record the subscription configuration, the GPO that enrolls sources, the first forwarded events per source, and a received router deny entry.

quizzes.question: Why source-initiated subscriptions rather than the collector pulling?
answers: Pulling is impossible on Windows
Sources push to one known collector, so no account with read-everything rights roams the network
Push is the only mode GPO supports
quizzes.explanation: Collector-initiated collection needs a credential that can read every source — exactly the kind of credential tiering just eliminated.

quizzes.question: What joins the Windows events on this host?
answers: Internet threat feeds
The workstation fleet's browsing history
The core router's deny log over syslog
quizzes.explanation: The boundary's refusals are evidence too. Landing them beside the sign-in record lets analysis correlate both views.

quizzes.question: How do you know a forwarded event really came from DC02?
answers: The MachineName on the event record in Forwarded Events
All events look identical
The collector renames events randomly
quizzes.explanation: Forwarded events keep their source identity — which is what makes the central copy usable as a record at all.

recap: Sources push by subscription; the collector reaches into nothing.
DC, admin-host, and router records land in one place.
Only registered paths carry the pipeline.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 gives the record its protected home.

lessons.title: Protect the record on SBD-AUDIT01
lessons.summary: The repository is where the record outlives mistakes and attackers alike: scheduled archives from the collector, hashed on arrival, readable by few, deletable by process only.
objectives: Archive the collector's logs to the repository on schedule.
Hash and catalog every archive on arrival.
Enforce the read-few, delete-by-process-only access model.
steps: Create the archival job: on schedule, the collector exports its Forwarded Events and syslog intake to dated archive files and transfers them to SBD-AUDIT01's repository share — the only inbound write path the repository allows.
On arrival, hash each archive and append the hash to a catalog kept with the archives; an archive whose hash no longer matches is a finding, not a file.

Set the permissions to match lesson 1's decision: the archival process writes, a named auditors group reads, and no interactive account holds delete rights — retention-driven deletion runs as its own documented, logged process, administered only under the audit custodian's separate accounts.

Fill in the AU table with what now exists: where each stage's data lives, its retention clock, and who can touch it — this table is the kind of artifact course 2.2 shows joining the Body of Evidence for the audit controls.
lessons.command:
Get-ChildItem \\SBD-AUDIT01\LogArchive | Select-Object Name, Length, LastWriteTime -First 5
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 \\SBD-AUDIT01\LogArchive\*.evtx | Select-Object -First 3
icacls \\SBD-AUDIT01\LogArchive
lessons.check: Dated archives arrive on schedule with catalog hashes that verify, the permission listing matches the access model exactly, and the AU table reflects reality.
lessons.evidence: Keep the archival job definition, the hash catalog excerpt, the permissions output, and the completed AU table.

model.label: Turn an event into evidence, step 4
model.text: The collector writes a retained copy to SBD-AUDIT01.

quizzes.question: What does the hash catalog actually protect against?
answers: Disk space exhaustion
Silent modification — an archive that no longer matches its recorded hash announces itself as tampered or corrupted
Slow searches
quizzes.explanation: Integrity is only provable if you recorded what intact looked like. The catalog is that record.

quizzes.question: How does anything ever get deleted from the repository?
answers: Any administrator's right-click
The analysis system prunes it
Only the documented, logged retention process
quizzes.explanation: The point of the repository is surviving its administrators. Deletion exists — as a process with a log, never a privilege.

quizzes.question: Where does the AU table go after this course?
answers: Into the Body of Evidence for the audit controls — course 2.2 shows how artifacts like it are organized
Back into course 1.1, retroactively
Nowhere — it is decorative
quizzes.explanation: Where the records live, how long, and who reads them is precisely what the audit control family asks an assessor to verify.

recap: Archives land on schedule and prove their own integrity.
Readers are named; deletion is a process, not a right.
The AU table is written for the authorization path.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 puts a working copy in front of an analyst.

lessons.title: Analyze in SBD-SPLUNK01
lessons.summary: Analysis earns its place with three working searches and one alert: failed privileged sign-ins, the boundary's denies, and the health of time — questions this network can already answer about itself.
objectives: Index the collector's streams into the analysis system.
Build the first three searches against real events.
Create one alert with a named responder.
steps: Install the analysis platform on SBD-SPLUNK01 and bring in the collector's two streams — the forwarded Windows events and the router syslog — over the registered forwarder path; the repository stays out of this flow by design.
Build search one: failed sign-ins (event 4625) involving the tier admin accounts, grouped by source host — the tiering course's denials now have a dashboard.

Build search two: router denies by source VLAN and destination port — course 1.5's boundary, now trending; and search three: time-service events and offsets, so clock drift surfaces before Kerberos complains.

Turn the first search into an alert with a threshold, a named responder from the admin plane, and a written first-response step — an alert nobody owns is a log entry with extra steps. Console access to all of this: VLAN 60 only, per the handoff.
lessons.command:
Test-NetConnection SBD-SPLUNK01.sbd.test -Port 9997
# In the analysis console, confirm the three saved searches return today's events
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4625} -MaxEvents 3 | Select-Object TimeCreated, MachineName
lessons.check: Both streams index with correct timestamps, the three searches return real current events, and the alert fires in a test with its responder and first step documented.
lessons.evidence: Record the input configuration, each search with a result sample, and the alert definition with its responder.

model.label: Turn an event into evidence, step 3
model.text: The collector forwards events to SBD-SPLUNK01 for investigation.

quizzes.question: Why does the repository stay out of the analysis flow?
answers: The protected copy's integrity never depends on the search tier — analysis reads the working stream, not the record
Splunk cannot read archives
Repositories are read-only hardware
quizzes.explanation: Lesson 1's separation, now visible in the plumbing: question the working copy freely; the record stays untouched.

quizzes.question: What makes an alert real rather than decorative?
answers: A red icon
A named responder and a written first step
Firing at least hourly
quizzes.explanation: Detection without ownership is noise. The responder and the first step are what turn a search into a control.

quizzes.question: Why is a time-health search in the first three?
answers: Clocks are easy to chart
Dashboards need a third panel
Drift breaks Kerberos quietly — course 1.5 built the clock, this search watches it
quizzes.explanation: The pipeline watches the dependencies the network actually has. Time is one failure that looks like everything else until you chart it.

recap: Two streams indexed; the protected record untouched.
Three searches answer real questions from day one.
One alert, one responder, one written first step.
lessons.next: The final lesson proves the chain end to end and runs the scans.

lessons.title: Prove the chain and delta scan
lessons.summary: One deliberate event, followed all the way: a failed privileged sign-in should appear on the source, the collector, the repository's next archive, and the analyst's screen — then the cadence scans close the course.
objectives: Trace a test event through all three stages.
Verify the router-deny stream the same way.
Baseline the new hosts and file the course evidence.
steps: Generate the test event: one failed sign-in on a DC with a wrong password for a tier admin account. Find it in the DC's Security log, in Forwarded Events on the collector, flag it for the next archive's verification on the repository, and watch the alert fire in analysis.
Repeat with the boundary: probe one unregistered port, then find that deny in the syslog stream and in search two — course 1.5's evidence pair now assembles itself.

Run the cadence: first baselines for SBD-SYSLOG01, SBD-AUDIT01, and SBD-SPLUNK01 (Windows hosts with the standard benchmark; SBD-SPLUNK01 runs Linux, so scan it with the DISA STIG benchmark for its distribution), plus a DC rescan for the audit-policy deltas.
File the end-to-end trace as this course's signature evidence and write the handoff: the fleet course inherits a pipeline that will see its first domain join happen.
lessons.command:
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='ForwardedEvents'; Id=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Select-Object TimeCreated, MachineName
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\logging-pipeline -Recurse | Select-Object Name, LastWriteTime
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\logging-pipeline\*
lessons.check: The test event appears at every stage with consistent timestamps, the deny trace matches, the new hosts have baselines, and the DC rescan deltas are attributed to the audit policy.
lessons.evidence: Keep the four-stage trace of the test event, the deny trace, the scan set, and the handoff note to course 1.9.

quizzes.question: What does the single traced event prove that stage-by-stage checks don't?
answers: That events have timestamps
That the stages connect — one real event surviving source to analyst is the pipeline working as a system
That 4625 exists
quizzes.explanation: Components can each pass while the chain fails. The traced event is the integration test.

quizzes.question: How is SBD-SPLUNK01, a domain-joined Linux server, scanned in this lab?
answers: It is exempt from evidence
With the Windows Server benchmark anyway
With the DISA STIG benchmark for its Linux distribution, on the same cadence as the Windows servers
quizzes.explanation: Linux distributions have their own DISA STIGs and Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) content. A domain-joined Linux server is held to the same scan cadence as every other server.

quizzes.question: Why insist the pipeline exists before the fleet course?
answers: So fifty domain joins happen in view of the pipeline — observed from the first boot instead of retrofitted later
Fleets cannot join without Splunk
DHCP requires a SIEM
quizzes.explanation: The ordering argument of this whole path: build the watcher, then the watched. Course 1.9 arrives to a network already paying attention.

recap: One event, four stages, consistent timestamps — the chain is real.
Boundary denies assemble their own evidence now.
Baselines, rescans, and the handoff to course 1.9 close the course.
lessons.next: That completes course 1.8. Course 1.9 brings in the fifty-workstation fleet — watched, addressed, and policy-managed from first boot.

prerequisites: Complete courses 1.5–1.8: routed network, working PKI services, DHCP with its relay, the tiered admin plane, and the logging pipeline.
Prepare a patched Windows 11 reference image (or template) for the fifty endpoints, obtained through the approved offline media process.

Confirm the Workstations OU, the container redirects from course 1.3, and the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Windows 11 Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) Group Policy objects (GPOs) from the course 1.3 package are ready to link.

Confirm the VLAN 80 access switch supports 802.1X port authentication, including a monitor (audit) mode that logs each result without blocking traffic. No new server is needed: the Network Policy Server (NPS) role goes on SBD-DHCP01.
labNote: Fifty endpoints join a network that is finally ready for them: addressed by DHCP, landed by OU redirect, hardened by policy at first boot, certified by autoenrollment, and watched by the pipeline from their first sign-in. The sample names run SBD-PC01 through SBD-PC50; match them to your own plan.

lessons.title: Prepare the fleet rollout
lessons.summary: Fifty of anything needs a factory, not fifty craft projects. Settle the image, the names, the join account, and the policy links so every endpoint is born identical — then prove it on paper before proving it on metal.
objectives: Finalize the reference image and naming plan for fifty endpoints.
Create a least-privilege join account scoped to the Workstations OU.
Link the Windows 11 STIG policies and the workstation firewall policy to the Workstations OU before any join.
steps: Finalize the Windows 11 reference image: current patches via the approved media process, no preinstalled extras, and a generalized state so each clone takes its own identity. Record the image version and hash — it is the fleet's common ancestor and belongs in evidence.
Write the naming and rollout plan: SBD-PC01–SBD-PC50, addressed by the course 1.7 DHCP scope, joined in waves (pilot of three, then batches) rather than all fifty at once.

Create a dedicated domain-join account delegated only the create-computer-objects right on the Workstations OU — no broader privilege rides along with fifty join operations. The course 1.3 redirect already guarantees machines land in that OU.

Link the DISA Windows 11 STIG policies from the course 1.3 package to the Workstations OU now, so the very first pilot boots into the hardened state — and note that Windows 11's own secure defaults will already satisfy some checks, just as Server 2025 did.

Create the workstation firewall GPO (SBD Workstation Firewall in this sample) on the Workstations OU: Windows Defender Firewall on for every profile with inbound traffic blocked by default, and inbound rules that allow SMB (TCP 445), Remote Desktop (TCP 3389), and remote management (TCP 5985–5986) only from SBD-ADMIN-PC01 at 10.0.60.30 — course 1.10 adds SBD-NESSUS01 for credentialed scans. No rule allows SMB or Remote Desktop between workstations: traffic inside VLAN 80 never reaches the router, so this policy, not the course 1.5 router rules, enforces the register's peer denies.
lessons.command:
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Staging\Win11-Reference.vhdx
Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Identity 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
Get-GPOReport -Name 'SBD Workstation Firewall' -ReportType Html -Path C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\workstation-firewall.html
lessons.check: The image is hashed and recorded, the join account holds only the delegated right on the Workstations OU, and the STIG and firewall GPO links show on that OU before any machine exists in it.
lessons.evidence: Keep the image record with its hash, the naming and wave plan, the delegation report for the join account, the OU's GPO inheritance output, and the firewall GPO report.

quizzes.question: Why does the join account get only create-computer rights on one OU?
answers: Join operations fail with more rights
Fifty joins should carry the least privilege possible — a stolen join credential then creates computer objects, nothing more
Delegation is faster than Domain Admin
quizzes.explanation: Scale multiplies exposure. Scoping the account bounds what the rollout's most-used credential is worth to an attacker.

quizzes.question: Why link the STIG policies before the first machine joins?
answers: So every endpoint's first boot is already the hardened state — no window where an unmanaged machine exists
GPO links expire if unused
The OU cannot be created otherwise
quizzes.explanation: The redirect lands them in the OU, and the pre-linked policy means compliance from minute one — the course 1.3 design, now paying off at scale.

quizzes.question: What makes the reference image part of the evidence?
answers: Images are always evidence
It contains the domain password
Its recorded version and hash are what make fifty 'identical' endpoints a claim you can verify
quizzes.explanation: A configuration record for the fleet starts with the common ancestor. The hash is how an assessor — or future you — confirms descent.

quizzes.question: What stops one workstation from opening SMB or Remote Desktop to another?
answers: The router's access control lists
Each PC's own firewall, set by the workstation firewall GPO — traffic inside VLAN 80 never reaches the router
Nothing until course 1.10
quizzes.explanation: Two PCs in VLAN 80 talk through the access switch, so the router never sees their traffic. Each PC's Windows Defender Firewall enforces the register's peer denies, which Inside the Network shows as rules D01 and D02.

recap: One hashed image, one naming plan, waves instead of a big bang.
The join credential can create computer objects and nothing else.
The Workstations OU is armed with policy before it holds a machine.
Peer SMB and Remote Desktop are blocked by each PC's own firewall, set by policy before the first join.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 joins the pilot and inspects everything a first boot should bring.

lessons.title: Join the pilot and inspect first boot
lessons.summary: Three machines go first, and everything the path has built shows up at once: a DHCP lease through the relay, an OU landing, STIG policy, a DNS record — and the join itself appearing on the analyst's screen.
objectives: Join a three-machine pilot with the scoped account.
Verify lease, OU placement, policy, and DNS registration per machine.
Confirm the joins appear in the logging pipeline.
steps: Deploy SBD-PC01 through SBD-PC03 from the image into VLAN 80, let each take its DHCP lease, and join sbd.test with the delegated account — nothing about the join should require a privileged credential.

Per machine, verify the inheritance chain: the computer object sits in the Workstations OU (the redirect working), gpresult shows the STIG policies applied, and the secure dynamic DNS record exists on both DCs.

Confirm the deny side holds: a pilot machine cannot reach another pilot machine's SMB or RDP — the lesson 1 firewall policy refuses it on the destination PC, because traffic inside VLAN 80 never reaches the router — and cannot open anything toward VLAN 60, which the course 1.5 router rules deny at the boundary.

Find the three joins in the logging pipeline: the domain controller events for the computer-account creations should already be on the collector and searchable in analysis — the first machines this network has watched arrive.
lessons.command:
Get-ADComputer -SearchBase 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter * | Select-Object Name, DNSHostName
gpresult /r /scope:computer
Resolve-DnsName SBD-PC01.sbd.test
Test-NetConnection SBD-PC02.sbd.test -Port 445   # expected: TcpTestSucceeded False
lessons.check: All three pilots sit in the Workstations OU with STIG policy applied and DNS registered, peer SMB/RDP fails as designed, and the join events are visible in analysis.
lessons.evidence: Keep each pilot's placement, gpresult, and DNS proof; the peer-deny output; and the analysis search showing the three computer-account creations.

model.label: Sign in
model.text: A workstation gets its address, finds a domain controller, authenticates, and reads its policy.

quizzes.question: How does a brand-new machine end up hardened without anyone touching it?
answers: Windows 11 hardens itself completely
Redirect lands it in the Workstations OU, where the pre-linked STIG policies apply at first boot
The DHCP server pushes the STIG
quizzes.explanation: Three courses cooperate in that one moment: the 1.3 redirect, the 1.3 GPO package, and this lesson's pre-linked OU.

quizzes.question: Why test pilot-to-pilot SMB and expect failure?
answers: SMB is removed from Windows 11
The pilots are in different domains
Each PC's firewall policy denies peer SMB and Remote Desktop — lateral movement inside VLAN 80 is cut at the destination host
quizzes.explanation: Peer traffic is switched inside VLAN 80 and never reaches the router, so the register's peer denies (D01 and D02) are enforced by each PC's own firewall — the policy lesson 1 linked before any join.

quizzes.question: What does seeing the joins in analysis demonstrate?
answers: The ordering worked — the pipeline built in 1.8 observed the fleet's very first machines arriving
That Splunk licenses cover 50 hosts
Nothing; joins are not logged
quizzes.explanation: Build the watcher, then the watched. The pilot's appearance on the analyst's screen is the sequencing argument made visible.

recap: Three pilots: leased, landed, hardened, registered — untouched by hand.
Peer traffic fails by design; the denies are the fleet's first evidence.
The pipeline watched the fleet being born.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 gives every endpoint a managed local administrator.

lessons.title: Manage local administrators with Windows LAPS
lessons.summary: Fifty identical machines must not share one local administrator password. Windows Local Administrator Password Solution (Windows LAPS) gives each endpoint its own rotating secret, stored in the directory, readable by the people the tier model says may have it.
objectives: Prepare the directory schema and permissions for Windows LAPS.
Apply the LAPS policy to the Workstations OU.
Retrieve and rotate a managed password under the tier rules.
steps: Extend the directory schema for Windows LAPS (Update-LapsADSchema) and grant the Workstations OU's computers the right to update their own password attributes — a one-time Tier 0 action, performed from the jump host and recorded like any schema change.

Grant read access on the managed passwords to the Tier 2 admin group only — exactly the people SBD-ADMIN-PC01 exists for — and nobody else; the tier model decides who may know an endpoint's local secret.
Create the LAPS GPO on the Workstations OU: managed built-in administrator, the password complexity and age the plan sets, and post-authentication reset so a used password does not live on.
On a pilot, confirm the policy applied, retrieve the password from the admin seat, use it once, and watch rotation — one cycle, fully observed, is the proof the other forty-nine inherit.
lessons.command:
Get-LapsADPassword -Identity SBD-PC01 -AsPlainText   # from SBD-ADMIN-PC01, Tier 2 admin
Get-ADComputer SBD-PC01 -Properties msLAPS-PasswordExpirationTime | Select-Object Name, msLAPS-PasswordExpirationTime
gpresult /r /scope:computer
lessons.check: The schema holds the LAPS attributes, only the Tier 2 group can read passwords, the policy shows on the pilots, and one retrieve-use-rotate cycle is recorded.
lessons.evidence: Keep the schema-change record, the permission delegation, the LAPS policy report, and the observed rotation cycle.

quizzes.question: What problem does LAPS remove from a fifty-machine fleet?
answers: Slow sign-ins
One shared local administrator password — where a single capture would open every endpoint
Password complexity rules
quizzes.explanation: Identical images tempt identical secrets. Per-machine rotating passwords make one compromised endpoint worth exactly one endpoint.

The machine's primary user
The Tier 2 admin group, from its admin seat — the tier model decides

One full cycle is observed and on record.

Verify chain and live revocation from an endpoint.

quizzes.question: What governs widening the template from pilot to fleet?
answers: The course 1.6 change process — requester, reviewer, versioning, record
A quick edit on the CA console
Nothing; templates are self-service

The DHCP relay

answers: Logs expire otherwise
The CA deletes it weekly
