The CA's issued log joins the evidence.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 puts those certificates to work at the switch port, starting in monitor mode.

lessons.title: Admit only enrolled devices with 802.1X
lessons.summary: Until now, anything plugged into a VLAN 80 port got an address. With 802.1X, the switch asks each machine to prove who it is with the certificate it enrolled. This lesson turns that check on in monitor mode — every result is logged, nothing is blocked yet — because 47 PCs have no certificate until they join the domain; lesson 6 enforces it once the whole fleet has enrolled. No new server: the NPS role joins DHCP on SBD-DHCP01.
objectives: Add the Network Policy Server (NPS) role to SBD-DHCP01 for port authentication.
Configure Extensible Authentication Protocol–Transport Layer Security (EAP-TLS) with machine certificates on the VLAN 80 access ports, in monitor mode.
Prove the pilots authenticate and that NPS logs every result.
steps: Add the Network Policy Server role to SBD-DHCP01 and register it in Active Directory. Give it a server certificate with the Server Authentication purpose from the issuing CA. It handles port admission only; router logins stay the named local accounts from course 1.5, so the server stays in the member-server tier.

Add the VLAN 80 access switch as a RADIUS client with a long, unique shared secret, then create the network policy: wired 802.1X, EAP-TLS only, machine certificates that chain to the approved root and carry the Client Authentication purpose, from the Domain Computers group.

Create quarantine VLAN 90 with no gateway and no routes and set it as the ports' failure and guest VLAN, but enable 802.1X on the VLAN 80 access ports in monitor (audit) mode: the switch runs every authentication and reports the result, yet keeps forwarding on VLAN 80 whatever the outcome (vendors name this mode differently). The other 47 PCs have no machine certificate until they join the domain in lesson 6, so enforcing now would strand them in VLAN 90, with no route to a domain controller. Push the wired 802.1X client settings to the Workstations OU by Group Policy (Wired AutoConfig, EAP-TLS, the approved root as the trusted CA).

Prove monitor mode with the pilots: each authenticates with EAP-TLS and NPS logs a grant (event 6272), while a failed attempt is logged — as event 6273 when the request reaches NPS — but still forwards on VLAN 80. Add register row F20 with its owner, and confirm the NPS events reach the course 1.8 collector through the existing event forwarding subscription.
lessons.command:
# On an enrolled pilot: the wired interface authenticated with EAP-TLS.
netsh lan show interfaces
# On SBD-DHCP01: recent NPS grants (6272) and denials (6273).
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=6272,6273} -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id
lessons.check: Every pilot authenticates with EAP-TLS and NPS logs the grant (6272); a failed authentication is logged but, in monitor mode, the port still forwards on VLAN 80; the ports name VLAN 90 as their failure VLAN; and the NPS events appear in the collector.
lessons.evidence: Keep the network policy export, the RADIUS client list (without the secret), the monitor-mode port configuration, the pilots' grant events and the failed test, and the F20 register row.

model.label: SBD-DHCP01

quizzes.question: Once 802.1X is enforced, what lets a workstation onto a VLAN 80 port?
answers: Knowing a shared password
Its machine certificate, checked by NPS through EAP-TLS
Being plugged in before the switch boots

quizzes.question: Once enforcement is on in lesson 6, where does an unknown device end up?
answers: Quarantine VLAN 90, which has no routes
VLAN 80, with a warning
The domain controller VLAN, so it can enroll
quizzes.explanation: The failure VLAN gives an unknown device a place to be that leads nowhere: VLAN 90 has no gateway, so nothing it sends is routed.

answers: NPS cannot authenticate people
Router logins need a separate license
If it authenticated the router's administrators, it could control Tier 0 and would have to be managed as Tier 0
quizzes.explanation: Anything that can control a Tier 0 system is Tier 0. Keeping NPS to port admission keeps SBD-DHCP01 in the member-server tier.

quizzes.question: Why does this lesson start 802.1X in monitor mode instead of enforcing it?
answers: Monitor mode is faster
The other 47 PCs have no machine certificate until they join the domain; enforcing now would strand them in VLAN 90, where they could never reach a domain controller
NPS cannot enforce on wired ports
quizzes.explanation: A PC enrolls its certificate only after it joins, and it can join only if the port lets it reach a domain controller. Monitor mode proves the configuration with the pilots without locking the rest of the fleet out.

recap: 802.1X runs on every VLAN 80 port in monitor mode: every result is logged, nothing is blocked yet.
The pilots authenticate with machine certificates; enforcement waits until the whole fleet has enrolled.
No new server: NPS runs on SBD-DHCP01, and its decisions are logged with everything else.
lessons.next: Lesson 6 scales from three machines to fifty, then switches the ports to enforcement.

lessons.title: Scale to fifty, enforce 802.1X, and prove by sample
lessons.summary: Roll the remaining waves while the ports are still in monitor mode, confirm every PC enrolled its machine certificate and authenticates, then switch the ports to enforcement — and prove the fleet the only honest way at scale: a defined sample, the same checks as the pilot, and a written rule for what a sample failure means.
objectives: Roll out the remaining endpoints in planned waves.
Confirm fleet-wide enrollment, then enforce 802.1X and prove an unenrolled device is quarantined.
Verify a defined sample against the pilot's full check set and widen event forwarding to the fleet.
steps: Deploy the remaining machines in the planned waves while the VLAN 80 ports are still in monitor mode, watching the DHCP scope's utilization and the join events arriving in analysis as each wave lands — the pipeline is now the rollout's progress bar.

Confirm every PC enrolled its machine certificate and authenticates: compare the issuing CA's issued certificates and the NPS grant events (6272) against the fifty computer objects, and fix any machine that is missing before going further.

Switch the VLAN 80 access ports from monitor mode to enforcement, and prove it both ways: an enrolled PC still authenticates and gets its normal lease, and an unenrolled test laptop lands in quarantine VLAN 90 and reaches nothing. Record the switch's port status and the NPS events for both.

Define the sample before checking it: for example one machine per wave plus any machine that logged an error — then run the pilot's full set on each sampled host (OU, policy, DNS, LAPS, certificate, 802.1X admission, peer-deny).
Write the sample rule down: one failed check in the sample widens the sample; a repeated failure stops the rollout and becomes a finding. A sample without a failure rule is a formality.
Extend the course 1.8 forwarding subscription to the Workstations OU so all fifty endpoints report their security events — and confirm fleet sign-ins now appear in the analyst's searches.
lessons.command:
(Get-ADComputer -SearchBase 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter *).Count
# On SBD-DHCP01: authentication results in the last hour (6272 granted, 6273 denied).
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=6272,6273; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Group-Object Id | Select-Object Name, Count
Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -ScopeId 10.0.80.0 | Select-Object PercentageInUse, AddressesInUse
Get-WinEvent -LogName ForwardedEvents -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object MachineName, Id
lessons.check: Fifty computer objects sit in the Workstations OU, every PC enrolled and authenticates, the ports enforce 802.1X with the unenrolled laptop quarantined in VLAN 90, scope utilization matches the rollout, every sampled host passes the full check set, and fleet events flow through the pipeline.
lessons.evidence: Keep the wave log, the enrollment reconciliation, the enforcement change with both admission results and their records, the sample definition with its failure rule, the per-sample check results, and the widened subscription proof.

quizzes.question: Why prove the fleet by sample instead of checking all fifty by hand?

Checking is impossible on Windows 11
Only pilots can be checked

The written rule: failures widen the sample, repeats stop the rollout and become findings
Rebooting twice
quizzes.explanation: The rule was written before the checks ran — which is exactly what makes acting on it defensible.

quizzes.question: What is the pipeline's role during the rollout itself?
answers: It pauses to save disk
It only matters after completion
Live progress and anomaly surface — each wave's joins and errors appear as they happen
quizzes.explanation: Course 1.8's investment turns deployment into something observed, not something reconstructed afterward.

quizzes.question: When is it safe to switch the VLAN 80 ports from monitor mode to enforcement?
answers: As soon as the first pilot authenticates
Once every PC has enrolled its machine certificate and authenticates in monitor mode
Never; monitor mode is enough
quizzes.explanation: Enforce only after the whole fleet has proven it authenticates. Then a missing certificate cannot strand a machine in VLAN 90, and every unknown device that appears later is quarantined.

recap: Fifty machines, rolled in waves, watched as they landed.
Every PC enrolled before enforcement; an unenrolled device now lands in VLAN 90.
A defined sample with a failure rule carried the proof, and the fleet reports into the pipeline.

The router's config export
The Windows 11 STIG benchmark — the fleet's own standard from the same DISA package

answers: Fifty enrollments changed its operational posture — change-triggered means this too
CAs are rescanned weekly by rule
It was missed earlier

Updates, endpoint protection, and vulnerability coverage — course 1.10's entire agenda
Network addresses

lessons.title: Design the rings and the software rules
lessons.summary: Decide how change reaches the network before any of it does: update rings that try things on the expendable before the essential, one approved source per software type, and register rows for every new path.
objectives: Define the update rings and their order.
Set the one-approved-source rule per software type.
Register the course's service paths.
steps: Define three rings and their order: a pilot ring (the course 1.9 sample machines plus one member server), the broad ring (fleet and member servers), and the critical ring last (domain controllers and both VLAN 30 hosts) — updates earn their way up, never down.

Write the software rule: Windows updates come only from SBD-WSUS01, Linux packages only from SBD-REPO01, protection definitions only through SBD-EPO01, and anything else arrives as a documented exception — one source per type is what makes 'unauthorized software' a checkable claim.
Decide the air-gap feeding cadence: what content crosses on media, how often, hashed by whom — the course 1.3 transfer procedure, now on a schedule.

Add the register rows: every Windows system to WSUS (8530/8531), domain controllers included; the domain-joined Linux servers (SBD-SPLUNK01 and SBD-NESSUS01) to REPO01 (HTTP, GPG-signed packages); every Windows system's agent to Trellix ePolicy Orchestrator (ePO) on SBD-EPO01 on its agent-server secure port, TCP 443, with the agent starting each connection; and the scanner's credentialed reach into each VLAN (SMB 445 and WMI to Windows, SSH 22 to Linux) — the one deliberate wide permit, owned and logged.
lessons.command:
# Capture the before state: where machines currently look for updates (nowhere internal yet).
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-ADComputer -Filter * -SearchBase 'OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' | Measure-Object
lessons.check: The ring table names every system's ring, the one-source rule and feeding cadence are written, and the register carries the course's rows with owners.
lessons.evidence: Keep the ring assignments, the software source rules, the feeding cadence, and the new register rows.

quizzes.question: Why do domain controllers sit in the last ring?
answers: They update fastest
A bad update should burn a pilot machine, not the identity fabric — criticality decides order
DCs cannot be updated
quizzes.explanation: Rings are a blast-radius design: change proves itself on what the network can lose before touching what it cannot.

quizzes.question: What does one-approved-source-per-type actually buy?
answers: Cheaper licensing
Faster downloads
'Unauthorized software' becomes checkable — anything not from the named source is a finding by definition
quizzes.explanation: A rule you can test is a control; a preference you cannot is a hope. One source per type draws the testable line.

quizzes.question: Which register row in this course is deliberately wide, and what disciplines it?
answers: The scanner's credentialed reach — owned, logged, and justified as the cadence's instrument
The fleet's path to WSUS
There are no wide rows
quizzes.explanation: A vulnerability scanner must reach broadly to be worth having. The register makes that breadth a documented decision, not an accident.

recap: Pilot → broad → critical: updates earn their way up.
One named source per software type, exceptions documented.
Every path — including the scanner's wide one — is a register row.

lessons.title: Build SBD-WSUS01 and the ring policies
lessons.summary: WSUS becomes the only road Windows updates travel: content imported across the air gap, approvals per ring, and Group Policy objects (GPOs) that point every OU at the server — with a pilot ring that proves each approval first.
objectives: Install WSUS and import content through the offline process.
Map rings to WSUS groups and OU-linked policies.
Approve and verify a first update cycle through the pilot ring.
steps: Install the WSUS role on SBD-WSUS01, scope its products and classifications to what the network actually runs — Windows Server 2025, Windows 11, and defender definitions — and nothing speculative. Microsoft announced in September 2024 that WSUS is deprecated and no longer actively developed, but it is still included in Windows Server 2025 and supported for production deployments, with security and quality updates under the product lifecycle.
Feed it offline: export the needed content on the connected side, hash it, carry it across, and import — the WSUS offline servicing path is the course 1.3 media procedure wearing an update hat.

Create WSUS computer groups matching the rings, and link ring GPOs at the OUs: update source SBD-WSUS01, the ring's group assignment, and install/restart windows that respect what each ring does for a living. The critical ring's GPO links to the Domain Controllers and Tier 0 Servers OUs.

Approve one update cycle for the pilot ring only, watch it install and report, then promote the approval ring by ring — the critical ring installs only what two rings already survived. Pilot and broad-ring approvals are Tier 1 work from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01; critical-ring approvals for the domain controllers and the two Tier 0 servers are Tier 0 work from AdminJumpBox01. Add SBD-WSUS01 to the SBD Tier 0 Console Hosts group and restart it so the new membership applies: the console reaches the server as a Kerberos network logon, the one Tier 0 logon type course 1.7's deny policy leaves open there, as its exception record states.
lessons.command:
Get-WsusServer | Get-WsusComputer -ComputerTargetGroups 'Ring 1 - Pilot' | Select-Object FullDomainName, LastReportedStatusTime
gpresult /r /scope:computer
Get-WindowsUpdateLog -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
lessons.check: Every system reports to its ring's group, the pilot ring installed and reported the first approved cycle, and the promotion to later rings followed the written order.
lessons.evidence: Record the product scope, the offline import with hashes, the ring GPO reports, and the first cycle's per-ring approval and install timeline.

model.label: Bring updates inside
model.text: Approved updates cross the air gap by hand, then members check metadata and pull signed content from SBD-WSUS01.

quizzes.question: How does update content reach this WSUS server?

By the approved offline export-import process — hashed media across the air gap
It generates updates locally

The DC's own download speed
Survival in the pilot and broad rings first — approval promotes ring by ring

answers: Unused content is imported, stored, and reviewed for nothing — and every artifact crossing the boundary should earn its trip
WSUS breaks above ten products
Licensing forbids more
quizzes.explanation: In an air-gapped lab, every megabyte is carried by hand. Scope is both hygiene and respect for the boundary process.

lessons.title: Endpoint protection through SBD-EPO01
lessons.summary: Protection becomes a managed fact, not fifty local settings: the ePO server deploys agents ring by ring, policy comes from one console, and the fleet's protection state is something the dashboard can simply show.
objectives: Stand up the ePO server and its agent deployment.
Apply the protection and DLP policy baseline by ring.
Verify coverage and wire detections into the pipeline.
steps: Build SBD-EPO01 in VLAN 50, fed its definitions through the offline process on the lesson-1 cadence, with its console reachable only from the admin plane — the register row from lesson 1 carries the agents' check-ins, and with the agent's peer-to-peer and RelayServer features turned off, endpoints open no listener for the server (TCP 8081, UDP 8082).

Deploy agents to the pilot ring first, confirm check-ins, then follow the ring order through the fleet, the member servers, and the critical ring — the same earn-your-way-up discipline as updates. Agent policy for the domain controllers is a Tier 0 scope in ePO, changed only from AdminJumpBox01 with a Tier 0 account. Add SBD-EPO01 to the SBD Tier 0 Console Hosts group and restart it, so course 1.7's recorded network-logon exception covers that console.

Apply the policy baseline: on-access protection, the scan schedule, and the data-loss-prevention policy scoped to what the model's DLP role calls for — each setting a decision in the record, not a default accepted silently.

Verify coverage against the living inventory — every endpoint present and checking in — and forward the server's threat events into the course 1.8 pipeline so detections land beside everything else; a standard test file makes the whole path fire once, on record.
lessons.command:
Test-NetConnection SBD-EPO01.sbd.test -Port 443
Get-Service -ComputerName SBD-PC01 -Name 'masvc' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Status
Get-WinEvent -LogName ForwardedEvents -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object TimeCreated, MachineName
lessons.check: Every inventoried endpoint shows a checking-in agent, the policy baseline is applied and recorded, and a test detection traveled from endpoint to console to the analyst's search.
lessons.evidence: Keep the coverage-vs-inventory comparison, the policy baseline record, and the traced test detection.

The console's coverage reconciled against the living inventory — agents checking in, compared to machines that exist
The install media's label
quizzes.explanation: Coverage is a comparison, not a feeling. Lesson 4's inventory is the denominator that makes the claim checkable.

answers: One place to look: detections correlate with sign-ins and boundary denies on the same analyst screen
The console cannot store events
Syslog is faster than consoles

answers: Live from the vendor cloud
They never update in a lab
On the written offline cadence — the same hashed-media ceremony as everything else

Coverage is proven against the inventory, not assumed.
Detections join the pipeline — one screen tells the whole story.

lessons.title: SBD-NESSUS01 and the standing cadence
lessons.summary: The course 1.3 cadence grows its instrument: credentialed scans per VLAN on schedule, findings flowing into the pipeline and the Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) habit, and this course's five new systems getting their own baselines on the way out.
objectives: Stand up the scanner with least-privilege credentialed access.
Run the first full-network credentialed scan and triage it.
Fold scanning into the standing cadence and close the course's scans.
steps: Build SBD-NESSUS01 on Linux in VLAN 50, joined to the sbd.test domain with its time taken from both domain controllers, plugins fed on the offline cadence, with dedicated scan accounts — least privilege for credentialed checks, its use logged, its register row the deliberate wide permit from lesson 1. The account that scans the domain controllers is a Tier 0 credential, kept apart from the member-server scan account and used only for DC scan jobs. Allow the scanner through the host firewalls it must reach — on the fleet, add SBD-NESSUS01 to the course 1.9 workstation firewall policy for SMB 445 and WMI.

Run the first credentialed scan VLAN by VLAN against the inventory, and triage like the course 1.3 rescan taught: every finding becomes fix-now, documented deviation, or POA&M candidate — never unexplained.

Wire results outward: findings into the analysis pipeline for trending, the triage into the living exception record, and the scan schedule into the cadence — quarterly with the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) release cycle, plus change-triggered, now automated enough to keep.

Close this course's own books: baselines for WSUS01, REPO01 (config-export pattern), MGMT01, EPO01, and NESSUS01, rescans where agents and policies changed existing systems, and the handoff — the network now sustains itself; course 1.11 finally gives it something to serve.
lessons.command:
Test-NetConnection SBD-NESSUS01.sbd.test -Port 8834
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\patch-protect -Recurse | Select-Object Name, LastWriteTime
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\patch-protect\*
lessons.check: The credentialed scan covered the inventory with the scan account's use logged, every finding is classified, results and schedule are wired into pipeline and cadence, and the course's baselines and rescans are filed.
lessons.evidence: Keep the scan summary with its triage, the scan-account and register records, the cadence entry, and the course's scan set.

quizzes.question: Why credentialed scans rather than unauthenticated ones?
answers: They run quieter on the network
Logged-in checks see the real configuration state — patch levels and settings — instead of guessing from the outside
Credentials are required by law
quizzes.explanation: The cadence wants configuration truth, which only an authenticated look provides; the scan account's scoping and logging keep that power honest.

quizzes.question: Where does a scanner finding end up?
answers: In one of three classified places: fixed, documented as a deviation, or on the POA&M path
Deleted if inconvenient
In the scanner only
quizzes.explanation: The triage rule from 1.3 scales up unchanged: open items end classified, and the classifications feed the kind of records course 2.2 teaches you to assemble.

quizzes.question: What did this course change about the cadence itself?
answers: It ended the cadence
It moved scans to the fleet's discretion
It gave it an instrument — scheduled credentialed scanning makes the quarterly-plus-change rhythm sustainable
quizzes.explanation: Course 1.3 set the rhythm by hand; the scanner is what lets a real operation keep the beat.

recap: Credentialed, least-privilege, logged — the scanner earns its wide row.
Findings end classified and flow into pipeline and records.
This course's systems are baselined; the network now maintains itself.

lessons.title: Design the service paths and identities
lessons.summary: Four services, and before any of them exist: who talks to what over which port, which identity each service runs as, and which groups own access — the register and the directory answer all three before a role installs.
objectives: Write the register rows for every business service path.
Choose managed service identities instead of password accounts.
Define the access groups that will own each service's data.
steps: Write the service-path rows: fleet to FS01 (SMB 445); fleet to APPS01 on its licensing port, recorded per application; fleet to WEB01 (HTTPS 443); WEB01 to APPS01 for the application API (HTTPS 443); and APPS01 — and only APPS01 — to SQL01 (TCP 1433 with TLS). Add an explicit deny from WEB01 to SQL01: the web tier has no database dependency. All four servers share VLAN 40, so the router never sees their traffic to each other — each server's host firewall enforces those rows. Everything else toward VLAN 40 stays denied, including endpoint-to-SQL directly.

Register WEB01's Linux maintenance rows as well: packages from SBD-REPO01 only (HTTP with GPG-signed packages) and syslog over TLS to the collector, SBD-SYSLOG01 (TCP 6514) — the same paths the other domain-joined Linux servers, SBD-SPLUNK01 and SBD-NESSUS01, use. Course 1.10's repository row named only those two because WEB01 did not exist yet.

Choose the service identities: group managed service accounts (gMSAs) for the SQL and application services, so passwords rotate themselves — and note Windows Server 2025's delegated managed service accounts as the migration path for any legacy service account this lab later inherits.
Create the access groups under the course 1.3 Groups OU — per-share and per-application role groups — because permissions will be granted to roles, never to named humans.

Request the server certificates through the course 1.6 process: one SBD Server Authentication certificate each for SQL01, APPS01 (for its application API), and WEB01, enrolled from the template, with the publication site serving their revocation story.
lessons.command:
Get-ADServiceAccount -Filter * | Select-Object Name, Enabled
Get-ADGroup -SearchBase 'OU=Groups,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter * | Select-Object Name
Test-NetConnection 10.0.40.20 -Port 1433   # expected before build: TcpTestSucceeded False
lessons.check: The register carries every service row — the SQL path restricted to APPS01 alone, the WEB01-to-SQL01 deny, and WEB01's repository and syslog rows — the gMSAs and role groups exist, and the three server certificates are issued and recorded.
lessons.evidence: Keep the service-path rows, the identity and group design, and the certificate enrollment records.

quizzes.question: Who may reach SQL01 on 1433?
answers: Any domain member
WEB01 and APPS01
Only APPS01 — the application tier is the database's whole audience
quizzes.explanation: Browsers talk to the web tier, the web tier calls the application API, and only the application tier queries the database. The register encodes that chain — including an explicit deny from WEB01 to SQL01 — and denies shortcuts around it.

quizzes.question: Why gMSAs instead of a user account named svc-sql?
answers: The directory manages and rotates the password itself — no human knows it, nothing expires unnoticed
gMSAs run queries faster
Password accounts cannot start services
quizzes.explanation: Service account passwords are a classic standing weakness. Managed accounts remove the password from human hands entirely.

quizzes.question: Why grant access to role groups rather than people?
answers: Groups are alphabetical
Access follows the job: membership changes are one record, and permissions never accumulate on individuals
Permissions cannot hold user names
quizzes.explanation: Role-based access is what makes 'who can touch this data' answerable from group membership instead of archaeology.

recap: Every path is a row; the database hears only SBD-APPS01.
Service identities are managed accounts, not passwords.
Access belongs to roles; certificates are already in hand.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 builds the file service the fleet will actually use.

lessons.title: Build SBD-FS01 with least-privilege shares
lessons.summary: The file server is where access control meets daily life. Build the shares against the role groups, require SMB signing on the server instead of trusting client defaults, and make 'who can read this' a one-lookup question.
objectives: Create the shares with role-group permissions and no individual grants.
Confirm the SMB signing and encryption posture end to end.
Verify access and denial per role from the fleet.
steps: Build SBD-FS01 in the Servers OU and create the planned shares, granting NTFS permissions to the lesson-1 role groups only — share permissions stay simple, the filesystem carries the detail, and no named human appears in an access control list (ACL).
Enable access-based enumeration so users see only what their roles permit — the quiet UX of least privilege.

Confirm the SMB posture. Windows 11 version 24H2 Pro, Enterprise, and Education require SMB signing for both inbound and outbound connections, but Windows Server 2025 requires it only for its own outbound connections — so require signing on SBD-FS01 as well (RequireSecuritySignature in its SMB server configuration), and opt the sensitive share into SMB encryption. Verify both on a live connection from a fleet machine rather than assuming the defaults.

Test as members of two different roles from fleet machines: each sees and opens exactly its shares, the other's are invisible and denied, and the denial lands in the pipeline like every other refusal on this network.
lessons.command:
Get-SmbShare | Select-Object Name, Path, FolderEnumerationMode, EncryptData   # on FS01
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select-Object RequireSecuritySignature   # on FS01: expected True
Get-SmbConnection -ServerName SBD-FS01 | Select-Object ShareName, Dialect, Signed, Encrypted   # on the fleet machine, during the test session
icacls D:\Shares\Projects | Select-String 'SBD'
lessons.check: Shares grant to role groups only, FS01 requires signing, a live connection from the fleet shows Signed True — or, on the encrypted share, Encrypted True, where Signed reads False even though an encrypted connection is also signed — and the two-role test proves both the access and the invisible-denied behavior.
lessons.evidence: Keep the share and NTFS permission reports, FS01's signing setting and the live connection's signing/encryption output, and the two-role test record with its pipeline entry.

model.label: Open a file, step 3
model.text: A workstation presents its service ticket and opens the approved share on SBD-FS01.

quizzes.question: Where does the fine-grained permission detail live?
answers: In the share permissions
On the NTFS filesystem, granted to role groups — shares stay simple on top
In a spreadsheet
quizzes.explanation: The classic split: simple share grants, precise filesystem ACLs, and roles everywhere — auditable at a glance.

quizzes.question: What does the live Get-SmbConnection check prove that settings review doesn't?
answers: That the actual connection negotiated signing or encryption — posture in effect, not posture on paper
That the share has files
Nothing extra
quizzes.explanation: Defaults differ by edition and direction — Windows Server 2025 requires signing only for its own outbound connections — so the evidence standard of this whole path is observed behavior: inspect the connection itself.

quizzes.question: A user can't see a share their colleague uses. What is that?
answers: A replication failure
A help desk ticket to grant access immediately
Access-based enumeration doing its job — visibility follows role membership
quizzes.explanation: Invisible-unless-permitted is the designed behavior; the role group, not an exception, is the path to access.

recap: Roles own the ACLs; humans own role memberships.
Signing and encryption are verified on a live connection.
Both the access and the denial are on record.

lessons.title: Build SBD-SQL01 behind its applications
lessons.summary: The database runs as a managed identity, encrypts its connections with a real certificate, and answers exactly one caller, SBD-APPS01 — the narrowest audience on the network, by design.
objectives: Install the database service under its gMSA.
Bind the SBD Server Authentication certificate for encrypted connections.
Prove the one-caller rule: SBD-APPS01 connects; SBD-WEB01 and the fleet are refused.
steps: Install the database engine on SBD-SQL01 with the lesson-1 gMSA as its service identity — the install itself demonstrates the managed account working where a password account used to live.
Bind the issued certificate to the instance and require encrypted connections; the chain validates against pki.sbd.test like every other certificate on this network.
Create the application databases with role-based database access for the APPS01 application identity only — least privilege continues inside the engine, not just at its port.

Prove the audience: a connection from APPS01 succeeds encrypted. The same attempt from SBD-WEB01 is refused by SBD-SQL01's host firewall — the two share VLAN 40, so the router never sees it — and one from a fleet machine dies at the router with a deny-log entry. Turn on the host firewall's dropped-packet logging if it is off, so both refusals leave a record.
lessons.command:
Get-Service MSSQLSERVER -ComputerName SBD-SQL01 | Select-Object Status
# From SBD-APPS01, the registered caller: expected TcpTestSucceeded True.
Test-NetConnection SBD-SQL01.sbd.test -Port 1433
# From a fleet machine: expected TcpTestSucceeded False.
Test-NetConnection SBD-SQL01.sbd.test -Port 1433
# From SBD-WEB01 (Linux): expected to be refused or time out.
nc -zv SBD-SQL01.sbd.test 1433
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\services\sql01.cer
lessons.check: The service runs as the gMSA, connections are certificate-encrypted with a validating chain, APPS01's access works by database role, and both direct attempts fail with a record: SBD-WEB01's at SQL01's host firewall, the fleet's at the router.
lessons.evidence: Keep the service identity proof, the certificate binding and urlfetch output, the database role grants, and APPS01's successful connection paired with both refusals and their log entries.

model.label: Attack drill, step 5
model.text: A compromised SBD-WEB01 reaches for SBD-SQL01 and is refused at SQL01's host firewall: rule F14 denies it, because SBD-APPS01 is the only registered SQL consumer.

quizzes.question: What demonstrates the gMSA actually working?
answers: The service running under it — a production role started by an identity no human holds a password for
A password in the evidence folder
The account's description field
quizzes.explanation: The running service is the proof: managed identity in use, with rotation handled by the directory.

quizzes.question: Why does the database get a certificate at all?
answers: Certificates speed up queries
Connection encryption with a validating internal chain — the PKI path's work, consumed by a real service
SQL refuses to install without one
quizzes.explanation: This is the payoff moment for courses 1.4–1.6: a business service encrypting with a certificate the lab issued, published, and can revoke.

quizzes.question: What is the complete evidence for the one-caller rule?
answers: The register row alone
A diagram of VLAN 40
APPS01's successful encrypted connection plus the refused attempts from SBD-WEB01 and a fleet machine, each with its log entry
quizzes.explanation: Same standard as 1.5: the permit shown working and the deny shown refusing, each with its record.

quizzes.question: Why does SBD-WEB01's attempt on SQL01 never reach the router?
answers: The router is offline during the test
WEB01 and SQL01 share VLAN 40, so the traffic is switched inside the VLAN and SQL01's host firewall has to refuse it
SQL Server only accepts UDP
quizzes.explanation: Traffic between two hosts on the same VLAN never crosses the routed boundary. That is why the VLAN 40 rows are enforced by each server's host firewall, and why the WEB01-to-SQL01 deny is written down explicitly.

recap: A managed identity runs the engine; no password exists to leak.
Connections encrypt under the lab's own validated chain.
One caller in: SBD-APPS01. SBD-WEB01 is refused at SQL01's host firewall and the fleet at the router.

lessons.title: Build SBD-APPS01 and SBD-WEB01
lessons.summary: The application server and the internal web server complete the dependency chain: fleet to web, web to application, application to database — each hop a register row, the web tier hardened against its Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) guidance, and HTTPS served from the lab's own trust.
objectives: Stand up SBD-APPS01's licensing service and application API on their registered paths.
Build the domain-joined Linux Apache server hardened per its DISA Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG), serving HTTPS with the internal certificate.
Prove the full chain: fleet → web → application → database, with the web-to-database shortcut refused.
steps: Build SBD-APPS01 in the Servers OU and run both of its services under managed identities: the licensing service, verified from the fleet on its registered vendor port, and the application API on HTTPS 443 with its SBD Server Authentication certificate, answering SBD-WEB01 only. APPS01 is the network's one SQL consumer — and the template for any future service: identity, row, evidence.

Build SBD-WEB01 on Linux and join it to the sbd.test domain with SSSD, as SBD-SPLUNK01 and SBD-NESSUS01 are joined. Point its packages at SBD-REPO01 only, its syslog over TLS at the collector, and its time service at both domain controllers, and harden the web tier against DISA's Apache guidance — the server's assessable record follows the Linux pattern: hardened configuration exported and hashed, checklist items answered in STIG Viewer.
Install the SBD Server Authentication certificate with its chain and serve the internal application over HTTPS — the 2,048-bit key floor from course 1.6's templates applies here as everywhere.

Prove the chain from a fleet machine: the HTTPS page loads with a validating certificate, and its data travels fleet → WEB01 → APPS01 → SQL01, every hop a register row. Then prove the shortcuts stay shut: a direct attempt from SBD-WEB01 to SQL01 on 1433 is refused by SQL01's host firewall, and the fleet still cannot touch 1433 at all — three courses of design visible in one browser request.
lessons.command:
Test-NetConnection SBD-WEB01.sbd.test -Port 443   # from a fleet machine
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\services\web01.cer
Test-NetConnection SBD-SQL01.sbd.test -Port 1433   # from the fleet: expected False
# On SBD-WEB01 (Linux): domain membership, the API answers, the database does not.
realm list
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://SBD-APPS01.sbd.test/   # use your application's health path
nc -zv SBD-SQL01.sbd.test 1433   # expected: refused or timed out
lessons.check: The licensing path works as registered, SBD-WEB01 is domain-joined with SSSD and patches only from SBD-REPO01, the Apache host serves HTTPS with a validating internal chain from a hardened, hashed configuration, and the end-to-end request proves fleet → web → application → database with both shortcuts denied.
lessons.evidence: Keep APPS01's identity and path proof, WEB01's domain-join and repository settings, its hardened config export with hashes and checklist, the certificate validation output, the end-to-end chain test, and the refused WEB01-to-SQL01 attempt.

model.label: Use a web app
model.text: Resolve the name, verify the certificate, check revocation, and request the application on SBD-WEB01.

quizzes.question: Where do WEB01's packages come from?
answers: Any public mirror that responds
A USB stick from home
SBD-REPO01 — the one approved source the 1.10 rule named for Linux software
quizzes.explanation: The one-source rule follows software wherever it runs; the web tier installs only what crossed the boundary through the repository, on the row lesson 1 registered for it.

quizzes.question: What is the Apache host's assessable record?
answers: A screenshot of the home page
Its hardened configuration export with hashes plus the answered STIG checklist — the established Linux pattern
Its uptime counter
quizzes.explanation: The router, the repository, and now the web tier: no Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) automation does not mean no evidence standard.

quizzes.question: What does one successful page load from the fleet actually demonstrate?
answers: The whole designed chain — the registered fleet-to-web path, validating internal HTTPS, the web tier's call to the application API, and the application tier's registered path into the database
Only that Apache started
That the fleet can reach the database directly
quizzes.explanation: The request traverses three register rows (fleet to WEB01, WEB01 to APPS01, APPS01 to SQL01) and the PKI in one go — which is why it is the lesson's closing test.

quizzes.question: SBD-WEB01 tries SQL01 directly on 1433. What happens, and why?
answers: It connects, because both servers sit in VLAN 40
SQL01's host firewall refuses it: WEB01 has no database dependency, and APPS01 is the only registered SQL consumer
The router drops it at the core
quizzes.explanation: The web tier reaches data only through the application API. The explicit WEB01-to-SQL01 deny, enforced on SQL01 because both servers share a VLAN, is what keeps a compromised web server from going straight for the database.

recap: APPS01 serves licensing and the application API; WEB01 joins the domain like the other Linux servers.
The web tier is hardened to its guidance and serves the lab's own trust.
One page load proves fleet → web → application → database; the shortcuts stay shut.

lessons.title: Reconcile, scan, and hand off
lessons.summary: The business services close the way every build course has: the register reconciled against live behavior, the new systems baselined, the inventory updated — and for the first time, the network is functionally complete.
objectives: Reconcile the full register against observed permits and denies.
Baseline the four service hosts and rescan what changed.
Update the living records and write the course's handoff.
steps: Run the full-register reconciliation one more time: every business-service row proven from its real source, every adjacent deny probed and logged, including WEB01 to SQL01 — the VLAN 40 section of the matrix joins the evidence beside courses 1.5 and 1.7's.

Run the cadence: SCAP baselines for FS01, SQL01, and APPS01; the config-export record for WEB01; a credentialed scan of VLAN 40 from SBD-NESSUS01 with its findings triaged into the three classifications.

Update the living records: the four hosts, their identities, certificates, and rings into the SBD-MGMT01 inventory; the new rows' owners into the register; any service-hardening deviations into the exception record.

Write the handoff: every modeled system except the recovery design is now built, watched, patched, and evidenced — course 1.12 proves the network can come back from the dead, and then path 2 takes the whole record to authorization.

Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\business-services -Recurse | Select-Object Name, LastWriteTime
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\business-services\*
lessons.check: The matrix covers every VLAN 40 row with paired permit/deny proof, the four hosts carry baselines or config records with triaged scan findings, and inventory, register, and exception record all reflect the finished services.
lessons.evidence: Finish the checklist: the reconciliation matrix, the scan and triage set, the updated living records, and the handoff note to course 1.12.

quizzes.question: Why re-run the whole register reconciliation now?
answers: The register deleted itself
Four services changed what the boundary must permit — the reconciliation proves intent and behavior still match after the biggest change yet
Reconciliations are decorative
quizzes.explanation: Each course's additions could silently break the last course's guarantees. The periodic full reconciliation is how the register stays true.

quizzes.question: What distinguishes WEB01's closing evidence from FS01's?
answers: WEB01 has none
FS01 is exempt from scans
FS01 gets a SCAP baseline; WEB01 gets the hashed config export and answered checklist — same standard, platform-appropriate instrument
quizzes.explanation: The evidence standard is constant; the tool varies by platform, exactly as the course has practiced since the router.

quizzes.question: What remains before the authorization path begins?
answers: Proving recovery — course 1.12 — so the Body of Evidence includes the network coming back, not just running
Nothing at all
Rebuilding the domain controllers
quizzes.explanation: A network that runs but cannot recover is half a story. The last build course makes restoration a demonstrated fact.

Every service host carries its platform-appropriate evidence.
One course remains: proving the network can be brought back.

lessons.title: Decide what recovery must prove
lessons.summary: Recovery starts as a list of promises: which systems and records must be restorable, how old a restored copy may be, how long restoration may take — written as commitments the rest of the course exists to keep.
objectives: Name the recovery set: what must come back, in what order.
Set the recovery point and time objectives per item.
Decide where backups live and who can touch them.
steps: Write the recovery set in dependency order — the same order the path built it: the directory first (everything trusts it), then the CA's database and keys, Group Policy, the router configuration, the log archive, and the living records themselves (register, inventory, exception record).

Set the two numbers per item: how much history may be lost (recovery point) and how long restoration may take (recovery time) — lab-honest values you will actually measure against in lesson 5, not aspirations.

Decide backup placement: each server's protected backup volume is written only by the backup process and readable by the recovery role, and a custodian carries copies to the offline backup cabinet on media — the air-gapped network's version of an off-site copy. There is no network path to the cabinet.

Confirm the standing custody items: the DSRM passwords are sealed and findable, and the root CA's protected backup from the course 1.4 ceremony is accounted for — recovery depends on secrets that must exist before the bad day.
lessons.command:
# Capture the current protection state before this course changes it.
wbadmin get versions
Get-ChildItem E:\Backups -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Measure-Object   # this server's protected backup volume
lessons.check: The recovery set is ordered by dependency with point and time objectives per item, the backup placement and access rules are written, and the DSRM and root-key custody records check out.
lessons.evidence: Keep the recovery requirements sheet, the objectives table, the placement and access decisions, and the custody verification notes.

quizzes.question: Why does the directory lead the recovery order?
answers: It has the most data
Everything else authenticates against it — services restored before identity have nothing to trust
Alphabetical order
quizzes.explanation: Recovery order mirrors build order for the same reason: the dependency chain starts at identity.

quizzes.question: What makes a recovery time objective honest?
answers: Making it very small
Leaving it unstated
Setting a value you will actually measure a rehearsal against
quizzes.explanation: Lesson 5 times a real restore. An objective nobody measures is marketing, not a commitment.

quizzes.question: What is the offline media copy for?
answers: Surviving a failure that takes the online backup with it — the air-gapped answer to off-site
Faster restores
Decoration for the evidence binder
quizzes.explanation: Replication and online backups share failure modes with what they protect. One custody-tracked copy stands apart.

recap: The recovery set is ordered by dependency, directory first.
Point and time objectives exist to be measured, not admired.
Backups get a protected home plus one offline, custody-tracked copy.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 makes the directory's safety net real.

lessons.title: Back up the directory, on schedule
lessons.summary: System state from both controllers, on a schedule, to the protected target — plus the quiet feature that handles the most common 'disaster' of all: the Recycle Bin for deleted directory objects.
objectives: Schedule system state backups on both domain controllers.
Verify and catalog each backup with hashes.
Enable the Active Directory Recycle Bin for object-level recovery.
steps: Schedule Windows Server Backup jobs on SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02 to each server's protected backup volume, including the system state and all critical volumes (wbadmin's -allCritical) so the same backup also supports a full server (bare-metal) recovery to different hardware — two controllers, two independent backups, because replication is availability and was never recovery (course 1.1's point, now kept).
After the first run, verify each backup's completion, record its version identifier, and hash the catalog entry into the evidence set — an unverified backup is a hope with a timestamp.

Enable the Active Directory Recycle Bin (a one-way, forest-level action from the Tier 0 seat, recorded as the change it is) so a deleted user or OU comes back intact without touching system state at all.

Write the restore decision tree: deleted object → Recycle Bin; corrupted DC on its own hardware → system state restore in DSRM (lesson 5's rehearsal); DC whose hardware is gone → full server (bare-metal) recovery from the critical-volumes backup; whole-forest loss → the Microsoft forest recovery guide, referenced and staged with the evidence rather than improvised on the day.
lessons.command:
wbadmin get versions
Get-ADOptionalFeature -Filter {Name -like 'Recycle Bin*'} | Select-Object Name, EnabledScopes
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\recovery\backup-catalog.txt
lessons.check: Both DCs show scheduled, completed system state versions on the protected target, the Recycle Bin reports an enabled scope, and the decision tree names the tool for each failure class.
lessons.evidence: Keep the backup schedules and version listings, the hashed catalog, the Recycle Bin enablement record, and the restore decision tree.

quizzes.question: Both DCs replicate — why back up both?
answers: Replication copies mistakes as faithfully as data; independent backups are the history replication doesn't keep
Backups run faster in pairs
Only one actually holds the directory
quizzes.explanation: The course 1.1 teaching point, finally implemented: availability and recoverability are different capabilities with different tools.

quizzes.question: An administrator deletes an OU by mistake. First tool?
answers: Rebuild the forest
The Recycle Bin — object-level restore with attributes intact, no system state needed
Ask users to recreate their accounts
quizzes.explanation: The decision tree's first branch: match the restore to the loss. Most disasters are small, and the small tool is already enabled.

quizzes.question: What makes a backup more than a hope?
answers: A long retention setting
Its file size
Verified completion, a recorded version, and a hashed catalog entry — and eventually a rehearsed restore
quizzes.explanation: The evidence standard applies to safety nets too: recorded, verifiable, and — in lesson 5 — actually exercised.

recap: Two independent system state schedules, verified and cataloged.
The Recycle Bin handles the everyday disaster in seconds.
A decision tree matches each failure class to its tool.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 protects the trust fabric and the supporting state.

lessons.title: Back up the CA, policy, boundary, and records
lessons.summary: The directory is not the only thing the network cannot re-derive: the issuing CA's database and key, the Group Policy set, the router's configuration, the log archive, and the living records each get their protected, cataloged copy.
objectives: Back up the issuing CA's database and key to its protected backup volume under ceremony-grade protection.
Refresh the Group Policy object (GPO) and router configuration backups into the protected set.
Fold the log archive and living records into the same catalog.
steps: Back up the issuing CA — database and private key — with certutil to SBD-SUBCA01's protected backup volume (E:\Backups in this sample), never to C:\Evidence: the private key is a secret, and secrets never go into evidence. Protect the key material to the same standard as the course 1.4 ceremony artifacts and record custody; only the backup's hashes and the custody record go into the evidence folder. The root's protected backup already exists from that ceremony and is verified, not duplicated, here.
Refresh the Group Policy backup (the course 1.3 Backup-GPO set, now the whole policy estate) and the router configuration export into the protected target, each hashed into the catalog.

Confirm the log archive's protection already satisfies this course — SBD-AUDIT01's hashed archives are themselves the record — and add the archive catalog to the recovery set so the evidence survives the systems it describes.

Export the living records — register, inventory, exception record, and this course's own sheets — into the set: a recovered network without its records would pass no assessment and teach the wrong lesson.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-SUBCA01: back up to the protected backup volume, never to the evidence folder.
certutil -backup E:\Backups\SBD-SUBCA01\ca-backup   # prompts for the password that protects the exported key
# Only the hashes and the custody record go into evidence.
Get-ChildItem E:\Backups\SBD-SUBCA01\ca-backup -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\recovery\ca-backup-hashes.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\recovery\gpo-backup\* | Select-Object -First 6
lessons.check: The CA backup sits on SBD-SUBCA01's protected backup volume with key custody recorded and only its hashes in evidence, the policy and router exports are current and hashed, and the catalog covers logs and living records alongside the systems.
lessons.evidence: Keep the CA backup's hash list and custody record (never the backup itself), the refreshed policy and router exports with hashes, and the complete recovery catalog.

quizzes.question: Why does the CA key backup get ceremony-grade handling?
answers: A copied issuing key is the power to mint trusted certificates — the backup is as sensitive as the CA itself
Keys are large files
certutil requires it
quizzes.explanation: Backups inherit the sensitivity of what they contain. The course 1.4 custody discipline applies to every copy of key material, forever.

quizzes.question: Why do the register, inventory, and exception record join the backup set?
answers: They are the largest files
A restored network without its records has lost its assessable story — the evidence must survive what it evidences
Backups require ten items minimum
quizzes.explanation: This path's real product is a defensible record. Recovery that saves the machines and loses the story saves the wrong half.

quizzes.question: What does this lesson do about the offline root's backup?
answers: Copies it onto the network for convenience
Ignores it
Verifies the ceremony-era backup's custody — it already exists, offline, and stays that way
quizzes.explanation: The root's protection is its isolation. This course checks the promise rather than breaking it with a networked copy.

quizzes.question: Where does the issuing CA's backup go?
answers: Into C:\Evidence, so assessors can inspect it
Onto SBD-SUBCA01's protected backup volume, with only its hashes and the custody record in evidence
Onto pki.sbd.test, beside the CRLs
quizzes.explanation: The backup holds the CA's private key, and secrets never go into evidence — the DNS course's rule. Evidence records that the backup exists and is intact: its hashes and its custody, not its contents.

recap: CA database and key: backed up to the protected volume, custody recorded, only hashes in evidence.
Policy, boundary, logs, and records all live in one hashed catalog.
The evidence now survives the systems it describes.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 moves the copies to the offline cabinet, by hand and on record.

lessons.title: Carry the copies to the offline cabinet
lessons.summary: A backup that sits on the server it protects fails with it. Move a copy of each backup to the offline cabinet by hand, under the same custody rules as any media crossing a boundary, and keep the custody record that proves it.
objectives: Define which custodian carries which backup, by tier.
Transfer the copies to offline media with hashes and custody records.
Prove a copy can be found, verified, and returned for a restore.
steps: Assign custodians by tier: a Tier 0 custodian handles DC system state and the issuing CA's database and key backup; the audit custodian handles the log archive from SBD-AUDIT01; a server custodian handles member-server backups. No one carries a tier they do not hold.
For each copy, write the media ID, hash the backup on its protected volume, copy it to encrypted removable media, and verify the hash on the media before it leaves the room.

Carry the media to the offline backup cabinet and record the handoff in the custody register: who, what, when, the hashes, and the storage slot. This is the course 1.3 media procedure used for backups.
Pull one copy back as a test: find it from the register, verify its hash, and confirm it is readable. Lesson 5's rehearsal restores from a copy that has made this round trip.
lessons.command:
# Hash on the protected volume, then on the media.
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 E:\Backups\SBD-DC02\*.vhdx
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 F:\Media-0012\SBD-DC02\*.vhdx
lessons.check: Every item in the recovery set has an offline copy with matching hashes on the volume and the media, a custody entry with a named custodian of the right tier, and one copy has been retrieved and verified.
lessons.evidence: Keep the custodian assignments, the hash pairs, the custody register entries, and the retrieval test record.

model.label: Offline backup & recovery
model.text: The offline cabinet has no network path. Copies arrive only by custodian under the media procedure.

quizzes.question: Who carries the domain controllers' system-state backup to the cabinet?
answers: Any server operator who is free
A Tier 0 custodian
The help desk
quizzes.explanation: A DC backup holds the directory's secrets. Whoever can handle it can rebuild or read the domain, so it stays with Tier 0.

quizzes.question: Why is there no network path to the offline backup cabinet?
answers: So ransomware or an intruder on the network cannot reach or encrypt the copies
Because backups are too large to send
Because NIST forbids network backups
quizzes.explanation: An offline copy survives an attack that takes the whole network. The custody record replaces the network path as the proof of what happened.

quizzes.question: The hash on the media does not match the hash on the volume. What do you do?
answers: Store it anyway and note it
Delete the original
Do not store it; recopy and investigate, because the copy is not trustworthy
quizzes.explanation: A mismatch means the copy is not the backup you verified. Storing it would put an untrusted copy where you will look on the worst day.

recap: Custodians carry only the backups their tier allows.
Every copy has matching hashes and a custody entry.
A copy has been retrieved and verified before anyone needs it.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 stops trusting the backups and tests one.

lessons.title: Rehearse a real restore, in isolation
lessons.summary: One restore, actually performed: a domain controller's system state brought back on the isolated segment, timed against the objective, verified against the directory — plus the small restore everyone will someday need, from the Recycle Bin.
objectives: Restore a DC's system state in Directory Services Restore Mode on the isolated recovery segment.
Measure the restore against the time objective and verify directory health.
Perform and record an object-level Recycle Bin restore.
steps: Stage the rehearsal: the isolated recovery segment has no path to the production VLANs — a restored controller believing it is authoritative must never meet the live directory; that isolation rule is written before the restore starts.

Restore SBD-DC02 from the offline copy retrieved in lesson 4, timing the work from decision to directory-services-running against the lesson-1 objective. A system state restore needs the same server instance — use a copy of SBD-DC02's virtual machine attached only to the isolated segment — started in DSRM: bcdedit /set safeboot dsrepair, restart, and sign in with the DSRM password. Restoring to different hardware needs a full server (bare-metal) recovery from the critical-volumes backup instead.

Remove the DSRM boot setting (bcdedit /deletevalue safeboot) and restart normally, then verify the restored directory the course 1.1 way — services, shares, a directory query. Record what the rehearsal taught: steps that surprised you, the measured time, and the decision-tree updates; then tear the rehearsal down completely.

Back in production, run the everyday restore: delete a disposable test object, bring it back from the Recycle Bin with attributes intact, and file both rehearsals — the big one and the small one — as the tested-recovery evidence.
lessons.command:
# On the isolated copy of SBD-DC02: start in DSRM, then sign in with the DSRM password.
bcdedit /set safeboot dsrepair
shutdown -t 0 -r
wbadmin get versions -backupTarget:<media-volume> -machine:SBD-DC02
wbadmin start systemstaterecovery -version:<version-id> -backupTarget:<media-volume> -machine:SBD-DC02
bcdedit /deletevalue safeboot   # then restart normally
Get-Service NTDS,DNS,Netlogon   # after restart, on the restored controller
Restore-ADObject -Identity <deleted-object-guid>   # production Recycle Bin rehearsal
lessons.check: The isolated restore ran in DSRM and reached a healthy directory within (or honestly against) the time objective, the DSRM boot setting is removed, the teardown is confirmed, and the production object restore returned the test object intact.
lessons.evidence: Keep the timed rehearsal log with its verification output, the lessons-learned and decision-tree updates, the teardown confirmation, and the object-restore record.

quizzes.question: Why must the rehearsal segment be isolated from production?
answers: To make the restore faster
A restored controller carries old directory state — meeting the live forest would inject the past into the present
Isolation is optional for labs
quizzes.explanation: The rehearsal's first rule protects production from the rehearsal. Old authoritative state on a live network is its own disaster.

quizzes.question: The restore took longer than the objective. What now?
answers: Hide the timing
Declare the objective met anyway
Record the honest number and either fix the process or revise the objective — both are legitimate; silence is not
quizzes.explanation: The rehearsal exists to replace belief with measurement. Either outcome — better process or truer objective — improves the real bad day.

quizzes.question: Why rehearse the Recycle Bin restore too?
answers: The most likely recovery event deserves the same tested-and-recorded treatment as the rare one
It is required before system state restores
Deleted objects expire daily
quizzes.explanation: Recovery evidence should match recovery reality: object-level loss is the common case, so its tool gets proven, not presumed.

quizzes.question: Your recovery host is new hardware. Which restore applies?
answers: A system state restore, exactly as on the original server
A full server (bare-metal) recovery from the critical-volumes backup — system state restores are for the same server instance
Copying NTDS.dit across by hand
quizzes.explanation: Microsoft's forest recovery guidance calls for a full server recovery when you restore to different hardware or a different operating system instance. A system state restore runs on the original instance, in DSRM.

recap: One real restore, isolated, timed, verified, and torn down.
The measured number replaced the hoped-for one.
The everyday restore is proven alongside the dramatic one.
lessons.next: The final lesson files the recovery record and closes the Build path.

lessons.title: File the recovery record and close the path
lessons.summary: The Build path ends the way it worked: owners, schedules, and evidence. The recovery record joins the living documents, the final scans snapshot the finished network, and the Body of Evidence is ready for the authorization courses to assemble.
objectives: Assemble the tested-recovery record with owners and review dates.
Run the closing scan snapshot across the finished network.
Hand the complete evidence set to the authorization path.
steps: Assemble the recovery record: the requirements and objectives, the backup catalog, both rehearsal results with the measured times, the decision tree, and a named owner with a scheduled next rehearsal — recovery is a practice with a calendar, not a binder.

Run the closing snapshot: the standing credentialed scan across every VLAN plus current Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) results per the cadence, triaged as always — the dated 'as-authorized' picture path 2 will reference.

Reconcile the three living records one final time — inventory against directory and leases, register against behavior, exception record against open findings — so the authorization path inherits agreement, not archaeology.

Write the Build path's closing note: what exists, where every record lives, and what is intentionally open — then start course 2.1, where this network stops being a project and becomes a system seeking authorization.
lessons.command:
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence -Directory | Select-Object Name
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\recovery -Recurse | Measure-Object
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\recovery\recovery-record.pdf -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
lessons.check: The recovery record is complete with an owner and next-rehearsal date, the closing snapshot is filed with triage, and all three living records reconcile cleanly into the handoff note.
lessons.evidence: Finish the checklist: the recovery record, the closing scan snapshot, the three reconciliations, and the Build path's closing note.

quizzes.question: What makes recovery 'a practice with a calendar'?
answers: A named owner and a scheduled next rehearsal — the test repeats as the network changes
Laminating the decision tree
Buying more storage
quizzes.explanation: One rehearsal proves today's backups. The schedule is what keeps tomorrow's honest.

quizzes.question: Why take a full scan snapshot at path's end?
answers: Scanners need exercise
It is the dated security picture the authorization decision will actually be about
To fill the evidence folder
quizzes.explanation: Path 2's assessors and the authorizing official evaluate a system at a moment. The snapshot is that moment, captured.

quizzes.question: What does path 2 inherit from twelve build courses?
answers: Just the virtual machines
A to-do list
A reconciled, evidenced system: inventory, register, exceptions, scans, and tested recovery — the Body of Evidence, already real
quizzes.explanation: The authorization path was never going to invent evidence; it organizes what the Build path produced on purpose, course by course.

recap: Recovery has an owner, a date, and a measured track record.
The closing snapshot freezes the as-authorized picture.
The Body of Evidence exists — path 2 assembles, it doesn't excavate.
lessons.next: That completes the Build the Network path. Continue with course 2.1 to carry this network — and its evidence — through the Risk Management Framework to an authorization decision.
